Surah Yusuf (upon him be peace) has 111 verses according to the Syrian reckoning and 112 according to the Meccan reckoning.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ "Tilka" (those) is a demonstrative referring to the verses of this surah, and "the Clear Book" is the surah. That is: those are the verses of this surah which were sent down to you, the verses of the surah whose matter is evident in its inimitability to the Arabs, or those whose truth becomes clear to whoever reflects upon them, that they are from Allah and not from men, or the plain ones whose meanings are not obscure to the Arabs because they were revealed in their tongue, or in them has been made clear what the Jews asked about, namely the story of Yusuf (upon him be peace). For it has been narrated that the scholars of the Jews said to the polytheists, "Ask Muhammad why the family of Ya'qub moved from Syria to Egypt, and about the story of Yusuf (upon him be peace)."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 2:

﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ That is: We sent down this Book, in which is the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, in the state of being an Arabic Qur'an. Some of the Qur'an has been called "Qur'an," because it is an ism jins (a generic noun, a noun of species) that applies to all of it and to part of it. ﴿So that you may understand﴾ that is, so that you may comprehend its meanings.

﴿And had We made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said: "Why have its verses not been made clear?"﴾ [Fussilat: 44]

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 3:

﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾ We explain to you the best of explanation. The qāṣṣ (narrator) is the one who relates the story according to its reality, from al-Zajjaj. It is also said that qaṣaṣ may be a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning iqtiṣāṣ (relating), as you say: qaṣṣa al-ḥadīth yaquṣṣuhu qaṣaṣan. It may also be a verb in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūl), like naqḍ (what is broken) and ḥasb (what is counted). According to the first meaning, its sense is: We relate to you the best of relating, ﴿by Our revealing to you this Qur'an﴾, i.e., by Our revelation to you of this sūrah. The word "aḥsan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (naṣb al-maṣdar) because it is in construction with it, and the object of relating (al-maqṣūṣ) is omitted, because "by Our revealing to you this Qur'an" suffices in its place. The meaning of "the best of relating" is that it has been related in the most original method and the most wondrous style; for you will not find its relating in the books of the earlier people comparable to its relating in the Qur'an. If qaṣaṣ is taken to mean the thing related, then its meaning is: We relate to you the best of what is related of narratives. It is best because of what it contains of lessons (ʿibar), wisdom (ḥikam), and wonders which are not found elsewhere. Apparently it is the best of what is related within its category, as one says: "So-and-so is the most knowledgeable of people," meaning in his field. The derivation of qaṣaṣ is from qaṣṣa atharahu, meaning he followed his trail, because the one who relates a narrative follows what he has memorised of it bit by bit. ﴿And indeed you were before it﴾: the pronoun refers to what We revealed, ﴿among the unaware﴾ of it. "In" is a light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form, and the lām is a distinguishing particle between it and the negative particle. The meaning is: indeed the matter and the account, you were before Our revelation to you among those ignorant of it.

**(When he said)** is a *badal ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion, *badal al-ishtimal*) for **"the best of stories"**, because the time includes the stories, or the implied sense is: "Recall when he said." **Yusuf (Joseph)** is a Hebrew name (*ism 'ibrani*), not an Arabic one, because if it were Arabic it would be diptote (*munsarif*, i.e., declinable with tanwin) rather than triptote-restricted, since it lacks any cause of non-declension other than being a proper noun. **To his father** Ya'qub (Jacob). **"O my father" (*Ya abati*)**: the reading of *abat* with the *ta'* is that of the Syrian reader (Ibn 'Amir). It is the feminine *ta'* (*ta' al-ta'nith*) that replaced the *ya'* of possession (*ya' al-idafa*) because the two are similar, since each is an added letter at the end of the noun. For this reason it is changed into a *ha'* when stopping (*waqf*). It was also permissible to attach the feminine *ta'* to a masculine noun, as in *rijlun rab'a* (a man of medium height). The *ta'* is kasra-vowelled to indicate the omitted *ya'*. Whoever vowels the *ta'* with fatha has deleted the *alif* of *ya abata* and retained the fatha before it, just as whoever deletes the *ya'* in *ya ghulam* (O boy) does. **"Indeed I saw" (*Inni ra'aytu*)**: from *ru'ya* (dream/vision in sleep), not from *ru'ya* (seeing with the eyes). **"Eleven stars" (*Ahada 'ashara kawkaban*)**: their names, as explained by the Prophet (ﷺ): "Jaryan, al-Dhayyal, al-Tariq, Qabis, 'Amudan, al-Fulayq, al-Musbih, al-Suruh, al-Farigh (p-95), Wathhab, and Dhu al-Kiftayn." **"And the sun and the moon"**: they are his parents, or his father and his maternal aunt, and the stars are his brothers. It has been said that the *waw* here means "with" (*ma'a*), i.e., "I saw the stars along with the sun and the moon." The stars were treated as rational beings in **"I saw them prostrating to me"**, because He described them with what is specific to rational beings, namely prostration. **The vision was repeated** because the first pertains to the essence and the second to the state, or the second is a new sentence (*kalam mustanaf*) in answer to an implied question, as if his father had said to him, "How did you see them?" and he replied, "I saw them prostrating to me," meaning humbling themselves; this is a *hal* (circumstantial clause). He was twelve years old at that time, and there were forty or eighty years between Yusuf's dream and his brothers' coming to him.

ÿ﴾Yā bunayya﴿ "O my son" — read with fatḥa on the yāʾ (bi-l-fatḥ) where Ḥafṣ is concerned, ﴿lā taqruṣ ruʾyāka﴾ "Do not relate your dream..." — ruʾyā has the same meaning as ruʾya (sight/vision), except that it is specifically used for what is seen in sleep (al-manām) rather than when awake (al-yaqaẓa), and the two are distinguished by the feminine suffixes, as in qurba and qurbā (nearness).

﴿ʿalā ikhwatika fa-yakīdū laka﴾ "...to your brothers, lest they plot against you." This is the answer to the prohibition: that is, if you relate it to them, they will plot against you. Yaʿqūb, upon him be peace, knew that Allah would choose him for prophethood and bestow upon him the honour of both abodes (this world and the Hereafter), so he feared for him the envy of the brothers. He did not say fa-yakīdūnaka ("they will plot against you") as in ﴿fa-kīdūnī﴾ "...so plot against me" [Hūd: 55], because the verb was given the sense of a verb that takes the preposition lām, so that it conveys the meaning of the act of plotting together with the implied verb, making it more emphatic and more forceful in warning. This is like: fa-yaḥtālū laka ("they will scheme against you"). Do you not see its reinforcement by the verbal noun, namely ﴿kaydan﴾ "a plot"? ﴿Inna al-shayṭāna lil-insāni ʿaduwwun mubīn﴾ "Indeed, Satan is to humankind a clear enemy" — evidently hostile — so he incites them to envy and plotting.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verse 6:**

﴿And thus﴾: like that selection (ijtiba') which your dream indicated, ﴿your Lord will choose you﴾: He will select you. Ijtiba' is an iftiʿal (the eighth verbal form, indicating reflexive or self-directed action) from *jabaytu al-shay'*, when you gather a thing for yourself, and *jabaytu al-ma'* *fi al-hawd*, when you collect the water in the pool. ﴿And will teach you﴾ is an independent sentence, not included in the ruling of the comparison, as if it were said: "And He teaches you" ﴿of the interpretation of events﴾: that is, the interpretation of dreams. Its interpretation (ta'wil) is its explanation and its exposition. Yusuf was the most skilled of people at interpreting dreams. Or it means the interpretation of the stories of the prophets and the books of God. *Ahadith* is an ism jam' (collective noun) for *hadith*, and is not the plural of *uhdutha*. ﴿And will complete His favour upon you and upon the family of Ya'qub﴾: by joining to them the blessing of this world with the blessing of the Hereafter, that is, by making them prophets and kings in this world and by bringing them to the lofty ranks in Paradise. *Al Ya'qub* means his family, which includes his descendants and others. The root of *al* (āl) is *ahl* (family), as evidenced by its diminutive *uhayl*. However, it is used only for those who have high standing, as in "the family of the Prophet" and "the family of the king," and one does not say "the family of the cupper." Rather, it is said "his family." Ya'qub knew that Yusuf would be a prophet, and that his brothers would be prophets, by inference from the light of the stars; therefore he said "and upon the family of Ya'qub." ﴿Just as He completed it upon your two fathers before﴾: meaning the grandfather and the grandfather's father, ﴿Ibrahim and Ishaq﴾, which is an ʿaṭf bayān (explanatory apposition) to "your two fathers." ﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Knowing﴾: He knows who deserves selection; ﴿All-Wise﴾: He places things in their proper places.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers﴾ — i.e., in their story and their account — ﴿there are signs﴾ — indications and proofs — ﴿of Allah's power and wisdom in everything.﴾ "Āyah" is Meccan. ﴿For those who ask﴾ — for whoever asks about their story and seeks to know it. And they are signs of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) for those Jews who asked him about it, and he informed them without having heard it from anyone and without having read a book.

Their names: Yahudha (Judah), Ruben (Reuben), Shim'un (Simeon), Lawi (Levi), Zabulun (Zebulun), and Yashjur (Issachar). Their mother was Layya, daughter of Layan. Dan, Naftali, Jad (Gad), and Ashir (Asher) were from two concubines, Zulfa and Balha. When Layya died, he married her sister Rahil (Rachel), and she bore him Binyamin (Benjamin) and Yusuf (Joseph).

The commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 8:

﴿When they said: "Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are,﴾ The lam here is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida', the emphatic lam), and it carries emphasis and affirmation of the content of the sentence. They meant that the excess of his love for the two of them is a established matter, without any doubt. They said "and his brother" although they too were his sons, because their mother was one and the same. "Ahabb" (dearer) was used for the two, because "af'al min" (the comparative form) does not distinguish between the singular and what is above it [the plural], nor between the masculine and the feminine, and a distinction is necessary only with the definite article (al-); when it is made definite by an annexed noun, both possibilities are permissible. The waw in ﴿while we are a band﴾ is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), meaning: he prefers the two of them in love over us, while they are young and lack capability, whereas we are ten men, capable, who attend to his needs. Therefore we deserve the increase of love more than they do, because of our superiority in number and in benefit to him. ﴿Indeed our father is in manifest error﴾ — an error in managing the affairs of this world. Had they described him as astray in religion, they would have disbelieved. "Al-'usbah" (a band) means ten or more.

"Kill Yusuf" is part of what is related after His words, "when they said" [Yusuf: 8]. It is as if they had all agreed upon this, except for the one who said, "Do not kill Yusuf" [Yusuf: 10]. It was also said: the one who commanded the killing was Shim'un, and the rest were content, so they were treated as having commanded it.

"Or cast him onto some land" — a remote, unknown, distant land far from inhabited places. This is the meaning of its being indefinite (nakirah) and stripped of description. Because of this vagueness, it was put in the accusative like the vague adverbs of place (zuruf mubhamah).

"So that the face of your father may be clear for you" — it will turn toward you with a single turning, not looking away from you toward others. The intended meaning is the purity of his love for you, free from sharing it with others. Mention of the "face" serves to depict the meaning of his turning toward them, since when a man turns toward something he turns his face to it. It is also permissible that "face" refers to the essence, as in His words, "and there remains the face of your Lord" [al-Rahman: 27].

"And [then] you will be" — jussive, conjoined to "so that ... may be clear for you."

"After him" — after Yusuf, i.e., after his being done away with by killing or banishment, or after his killing or casting away; the pronoun then refers to the verbal noun of "kill" or "cast away."

"A righteous people" — repentant turning to Allah from what you have wrongfully done to him; or, your condition will be made right in the sight of your father.

﴿A speaker among them said﴾ He is Yahudha (Judah), who was the best of them in opinion regarding him. ﴿Do not kill Joseph﴾, for killing is a grave matter. ﴿But cast him into the bottom of the well, and some travelers will pick him up﴾: in the depths of the pit, and what is hidden of him from the eye of the beholder. "Ghayabat" (in the plural, "ghayabāt") and what follows it are read by the Medinan reader (the Medinan reading). ﴿Some travelers will pick him up﴾: some of the groups who travel along the road. ﴿If you are going to do something﴾ with him.

(p-٩٨)

"They said: 'O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph, when indeed we are sincere well-wishers to him?' That is: why do you fear for him at our hands, when we wish him well and are concerned for him? By this they intended, when they had resolved upon a plot against Joseph, to draw him away from his opinion and his habit of guarding him from them. And in this is a proof that he sensed from them something that made him unwilling to trust them with him."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 12:

﴿Send him with us tomorrow, he will enjoy himself and play﴾ — "nataṣṣi‘" (we will extend ourselves) in eating fruits and other things; and "al-ratʿa" (the ratʿah, meaning abundance and ease). ﴿and he will play﴾ — "natafarraj" (we will amuse ourselves) with what is permissible, such as hunting, shooting arrows, and running. The reading with the letter yāʾ (يَرْتَعْ يَلْعَبْ in the yāʾ form) in both places is that of the Madani and Kufan readers; with the letter nūn in both places is that of the Meccan, Syrian and Abu ʿAmr readers; and with a kasra on the ʿayn (يَرْتَعِ) is that of the Hijazi reader, from "ارْتَعى يَرْتَعِي" (irtaʿā yartaʿī), which is an ifti‘āl form from al-raʿy (pasturing). ﴿And indeed we will be its guardians﴾ — from anything harmful reaching him.

He said, "It grieves me that you take him away," meaning: your taking him away grieves me. The lam here is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida', the emphatic lam). "And I fear that a wolf will eat him while you are heedless of him." He excused himself to them, saying that their taking him away is something that saddens him, because he could not bear to be parted from him for an hour, and that he feared for him an attack by a wolf if they were heedless of him while busy with their herding and their play.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 14:

﴿They said: "If the wolf eats him while we are a band,"﴾ The lam is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwatta'ah, the lam that prepares for an oath), and the oath is omitted; its implied form is: "By God, if the wolf eats him..." The waw in ﴿while we are a band﴾ — i.e., a group gathered together and capable of defense — is for the circumstantial (hal) clause. ﴿Indeed, then we would be losers.﴾ This is the answer to the oath, serving in place of the answer to the conditional clause. That is: if we are not able to protect one another, then our flocks have perished and we have lost them.

And they answered his second excuse but not the first, because that (the first) was what would enrage them. (p-99)

So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well (*ghayabat al-jubb*), i.e., they resolved to throw him into the well. This well was three farsakhs (parasangs) from the dwelling of Ya'qub (peace be upon him). The response (*jawab*) of *lamma* ("when") is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "they did to him what they did of harm." It is narrated that when they brought him out into the open desert, they showed him enmity, struck him, and nearly killed him, but Yahudha (Judah) prevented them. When they wanted to throw him into the well, he clung to their garments, and they pulled them from his hand. He then held on to the wall of the well, so they tied his hands and stripped off his shirt to smear it with blood, so that they could deceive their father with it. They lowered him into the well, which contained water, and he fell into it. Then he took refuge on a rock, stood upon it, and wept. Yahudha used to bring him food. It is also related that when Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was cast into the fire, he was stripped of his clothes, and Jibril (peace be upon him) brought him a shirt of Paradise silk and dressed him in it. Ibrahim passed it to Ishaq, and Ishaq passed it to Ya'qub, who put it into an amulet (*tamima*, a charm worn as protection) that he hung around Yusuf's neck. Jibril then took it out and dressed him in it.

﴿And We revealed to him﴾. It has been said that he received the revelation while still a child, just as Yahya and Isa (peace be upon them both) received it as children. It has also been said that by then he had reached the age of discernment.

﴿You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs﴾, i.e., you will tell your brothers what they did to you, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ that you are Yusuf, because of your exalted rank and the majesty of your authority. This is because when they entered upon him seeking provisions, ﴿he recognized them, but they did not recognize him﴾ [Yusuf: 58]. He called for the *suwa'* (royal drinking goblet), placed it on his hand, then struck it so that it hummed, and said: "This goblet tells me that you had a brother from your father called Yusuf, and that you threw him into the depths of the well, and told his father, 'The wolf has eaten him,' and you sold him for a paltry price."

Alternatively, the clause ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is connected to *awhayna* ("We revealed"), meaning: We gave him comfort through the revelation and removed the loneliness from his heart, while they did not perceive that.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 16:**

﴿And they came to their father in the evening﴾ — for concealment and for audacity in making excuses. ﴿Weeping﴾ is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause, describing the state in which they came). (p-100) It is narrated from al-A'mash: "Do not believe a weeping woman after the brothers of Joseph." When he heard their voices, he was alarmed and said, "What is the matter with you, my sons? Has something befallen your flock?" They said, "No." He said, "Then what is the matter with you, and where is Joseph?"

"They said: O our father, indeed we went off racing one another," that is, competing in running or in shooting. The form ifti'al (الِافْتِعالُ) and the form tafa'ul (التَفاعُلُ) are both used for mutual action, like irtima' (الِارْتِماءُ) and tarami (التَرامِي) and others. "And we left Yusuf by our belongings, and the wolf devoured him. But you will not believe us," that is, you will not accept us as truthful, "even if we were truthful." Even if we were among those known for truthfulness and trustworthiness in your sight, owing to the intensity of your love for Yusuf. So how much more so, when you have an ill opinion of us and do not trust our word?!

﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood.﴾ Kadhib (false) is either an attributive, meaning dhū kadhib (possessing falsehood), or it is described by a verbal noun (maṣdar) for intensification (mubālaghah), as if it were the very essence and substance of falsehood. This is like what is said of a great liar: "He is falsehood itself and lies in person," and "he is the lie in its very form and the falsehood in its essence."

It is narrated that they slaughtered a young goat, smeared the shirt with its blood, and forgot to tear it. It is also narrated that when Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) heard the news about Yusuf, he cried out at the top of his voice and said, "Where is the shirt?" He took it, placed it over his face, and wept until his face was stained with the blood of the shirt, and he said, "By God, I have never seen a wolf as gentle as this one, which ate my son and did not tear his shirt."

It was also said that there were three signs in Yusuf's shirt: it was a proof for Yaʿqub of their lie, and when he placed it over his face he regained his sight, and it was a proof of Yusuf's innocence when it was torn from behind.

The position of ﴿عَلى قَمِيصِهِ﴾ (ʿalā qamīṣihi) is accusative as an adverbial of place (ẓarf), as if it were said: "And they came above his shirt with blood."

﴿Said﴾ Yaʿqub (peace be upon him), ﴿"Rather, your souls have made a matter appealing to you"﴾, meaning adorned it or made it easy for you, ﴿"a [great] matter"﴾ that you committed. ﴿"So patience is beautiful"﴾ is either a predicate or a subject, since it is described: that is, "my affair is beautiful patience," or "patience is more beautiful." It is the patience in which there is no complaint to people. ﴿"And God is the one sought for help"﴾, meaning I seek His help ﴿against﴾ bearing ﴿what you describe﴾ of Yusuf's destruction and of patience in the face of the calamity concerning him.

[p-101] ﴿And a caravan came﴾, a company traveling from the direction of Madyan toward Egypt. This was three days after Yusuf had been thrown into the well. They lost their way and camped near it. The well was in a barren wilderness far from settlement, and its water was brackish, but it became sweet when Yusuf was lowered into it. ﴿Then they sent their water-drawer﴾, the one who goes to the water to draw for the people. His name was Malik ibn Dhu'r al-Khuza'i. ﴿So he lowered his bucket﴾, he sent the bucket down to fill it, and Yusuf caught hold of the bucket, so he pulled it up. ﴿He said, "Oh, good news!"﴾ The Kufan reading calls out "bushra" as if he were saying: "Come, for this is your time." Others read "bushraya," with the noun attached to his own self, or it is the name of his boy, so he called to him as an attached form of himself. ﴿This is a boy﴾. It was said that he took him away, and when he drew near to his companions, he cried out this to give them the good news of him. ﴿And they concealed him﴾. The pronoun refers to the water-drawer and his companions; they hid him from the company, or it refers to Yusuf's brothers, for they told the company, "This is a slave of ours who has run away; buy him from us," and Yusuf kept silent for fear that they would kill him. ﴿As merchandise﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: they concealed him as goods for trade. Bidā'a (merchandise) is the portion of wealth set aside for trade, i.e., cut off from the rest. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of what they do﴾, of what the brothers of Yusuf did to their father and their brother of evil conduct.

And they sold him for a paltry price, defrauded, deficient relative to its value by an evident deficiency; or: counterfeit, [for] ﴿dirhams﴾, which is a *badal* (substitute in apposition) for "price," ﴿counted﴾, few in number, counted by tallying and not weighed, for they used to count what was below forty and weigh forty and above, and it was twenty dirhams. ﴿And they were among those who were indifferent to it﴾, from among those who are averse to what is in their hand, so they sell it for the trifling price. Or the meaning of "and they sold him" and "and they bought him" is: the caravan (*rufqah*) of his brothers. ﴿And they were among those who were indifferent to it﴾, i.e., not desirous, because they believed he was a runaway. It is related that his brothers followed them and said: "Secure him, lest he run away." And "fīhi" (in him) is not a complement (*ṣilah*, the element completing a relative clause) of "al-zāhidīn" (those who were indifferent), i.e., not desirous, because the complement does not precede the element it completes (*mawṣūl*, the relative/governing word). Rather, it is an explanation (*bayān*), as if it were said: "In what did they show indifference?" and he said: "They showed indifference *fīhi*."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 21:

﴿The one who bought him from Egypt said﴾ He was Qatfir, and he was the Aziz (al-'Aziz, the minister or governor) who was over the treasuries of Egypt. The king at that time was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, and he had believed in Yusuf and died during his lifetime. The Aziz bought him with his finery, silver, silk and musk when he was seventeen years old. He stayed in his house for thirteen years, and al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid appointed him as his vizier when he was thirty years old. God gave him wisdom and knowledge when he was thirty-three years old, and he died when he was one hundred and twenty years old. ﴿to his wife﴾ Ra'il, or Zulaykha. The lam (لام) is connected to qala (قال, "said") and not to ishtarahu (اشتراه, "bought"). ﴿Make his stay honourable﴾ Make his station and his place with us honourable, meaning good and pleasing, as evidenced by His saying ﴿Indeed, He is my Lord; He has made my stay excellent﴾ [Yusuf: 23]. It is also reported from al-Dahhak that it means: make his livelihood good, his comfort gentle, and his bed comfortable. ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾ Perhaps, when he is trained and handles affairs and understands their courses, we will rely on him for some of what we are engaged in. ﴿Or we may adopt him as a son﴾ Or we may adopt him and place him in the position of a son. Qatfir was sterile, and he had perceived in him the sign of right guidance, so he said this. ﴿And thus﴾ This refers to what preceded of his deliverance and the turning of the Aziz's heart towards him. The kaf (كاف) is in the accusative, and its implied meaning is: "and in the same manner as that deliverance and that turning of heart." ﴿We established Yusuf﴾ That is, just as We delivered him and turned the heart of the Aziz towards him, so likewise We established him ﴿in the land﴾, that is, the land of Egypt, and We made him a king who disposes of it by his command and prohibition. ﴿And that We may teach him the interpretation of events﴾ That deliverance and establishment were [for this purpose]. ﴿And Allah is dominant over His affair﴾ He cannot be prevented from what He wills, or [it means] over the affair of Yusuf, by conveying to him what He intended for him, rather than what his brothers intended. ﴿But most of the people do not know﴾ this.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 22:**

﴿When he reached his full strength﴾: the limit of the maturing of his strength, which is eighteen years or twenty-one years. ﴿We gave him judgement and knowledge﴾: ḥikmah (wisdom), and it is knowledge together with action, and abstaining from what is done in ignorance; or judgement between people and fiqh (jurisprudence). ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾: an indication that he was a good-doer in his actions and God-fearing (muttaqi) in the early bloom of his affair.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 23:

﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself.﴾ That is, she asked Yusuf to lie with her. The word murawadah (seduction, persuasion) is a mufa'alah form from raada yaroodu, meaning "to come and go." The sense is: she deceived him concerning himself, that is, she did the act of one who deceives his companion regarding a thing he does not want to let go of from his hand, scheming to overpower him and take it from him. This is an expression for contriving means to make him lie with her. ﴿And she bolted the doors﴾, and there were seven of them. ﴿And she said, "Come, [I am] yours!"﴾ Hayt (come on) is a word meaning "come and approach." It is built on fatḥ (the vowel "a"). Hayta (with fatḥah on the ta) is the reading of Makki, who built it on ḍammah (the vowel "u"), while Hayta (with kasrah) is the reading of Madani and Shami. The lam is for clarification, as if it were said: "To you I say this," just as you would say: "Halumma laka" (come to you). ﴿He said, "I seek refuge in Allah"﴾, I seek refuge in Allah with a seeking. ﴿Indeed, He﴾, that is, indeed the matter and the account, ﴿is my Lord﴾, my master and owner, meaning Qitfir, ﴿who has made my residence good﴾ when he said to you: "Honor his residence." So what would be the recompense for this, that I should betray him concerning his family? ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾, those who betray, or the adulterers. Or he meant by his saying "Indeed, He is my Lord" Allah, the Exalted, because He is the Causer of causes.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 24:

﴿And indeed she desired him﴾ — a desire of resolve (hamm 'azm). ﴿And he desired her﴾ — a desire of natural inclination (hamm al-tiba') together with restraint. This is what al-Hasan said. Shaykh Abu Mansur, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "And he desired her" was a desire of passing thought (khatrah), and the servant has no role in what passes through the heart, nor is he held accountable for it. Had his desire been like hers, Allah would not have praised him by saying that he was among His sincere servants.

It was also said: "And he desired her" means he came close to desiring her (wa-sharafa an yahumma biha). It is said: "hamma bil-amr" when one intends it and resolves upon it.

The answer to ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ is omitted, meaning: "what had been would have been." It was also said that "and he desired her" is its answer, but this is not sound, because the answer of law (lawla) cannot precede it, since it has the status of a conditional and the opening of the sentence belongs to it. Al-burhan means the proof (al-hujjah).

It is permissible that "and he desired her" falls within the scope of the oath in His saying "And indeed she desired him," and it is permissible that it falls outside it. When the reciter takes it as outside the scope of the oath and as a separate statement, it is proper for him to pause at "bihi" (him) and begin with His saying "and he desired her." This also indicates the difference between the two desires.

The desire of Yusuf was explained as: he untied the drawstring of his trousers and sat between her four limbs while she lay on her back. The proof (al-burhan) was explained as: he heard a voice saying, "Beware of her, and beware of her," twice, then he heard a third voice, "Turn away from her," but it did not affect him, until Ya'qub appeared to him biting his finger-joint. This is false, and its falsehood is shown by His saying: ﴿She sought to seduce me from myself﴾ [Yusuf: 26], for had that also been from him, he would not have cleared himself of it. And His saying: ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾ — had it been so, evil would not have been turned away from him. And His saying: ﴿That he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾ [Yusuf: 52] — had it been so, he would have betrayed him in his absence. And His saying: ﴿We knew no evil of him﴾ [Yusuf: 51], and ﴿Now the truth has become evident; it was I who sought to seduce him, and indeed he is of the truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 51]. Moreover, had such a thing occurred from him, his repentance and seeking forgiveness would have been mentioned, as was the case for Adam, Nuh, Dhu al-Nun and Dawud, peace be upon them. Allah has named him "sincere," so it is known with certainty that he stood firm in that station and struggled against his self with the struggle of those of firm resolve, reflecting upon the proofs of prohibition, until he earned Allah's praise.

The place of the kaf in ﴿Thus﴾ is in the accusative: that is, "like that steadfastness We made him steadfast," or in the nominative: that is, "the matter is like that." ﴿That We might turn away from him evil﴾ — the betrayal of the master — ﴿and immorality﴾ — fornication. ﴿Indeed he is of Our sincere servants﴾ — with the lam vowelled with a fatha wherever it occurs, according to Madani and Kufi readers, meaning those whom Allah has purified for His obedience; and with a kasra according to others, meaning those who have made their religion sincere for Allah. The meaning of ﴿of Our servants﴾ is "some of Our servants," that is, he is one sincere among the body of the sincere.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 25:

﴿And they both raced to the door﴾. "Tasabaqa" means they raced one another to the door. The verb "istabaqa" takes "ila" (to), but here it is used with "al-bab" (the door) directly, which is a case of omitting the preposition and making the verb transitive, as in His saying ﴿And Moses chose from his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. Alternatively, "istabaqa" is taken in the sense of "ibtadara" (hurried to), by way of "tadmin" (the inclusion of one verb's meaning in another, a figure of speech). Yusuf fled from her and hastened toward the door, wanting to go out, and she hastened after him to prevent him from leaving. The word "door" is singular here, though in His saying ﴿and she bolted the doors﴾ [Yusuf: 23] it is plural, because he meant the outer door, the one through which one leaves the house. When Yusuf fled, the bolt's pieces began to scatter and fall until he got out (p. 105).

﴿And she tore his shirt from behind﴾. She pulled him from behind, so it was torn, that is, it split as he fled from her toward the door, and she followed him trying to stop him. ﴿And they found her husband at the door﴾. They came upon her husband, Qitfir, coming in, wanting to enter. When she saw him, she devised a plan to clear herself of suspicion in her husband's eyes, and to frighten Yusuf, hoping he would comply with her out of fear of her and her scheming. So she ﴿said: What is the requital for one who intended evil to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?﴾ Here "ma" is a negating particle, meaning: the requital for him is nothing but prison.

﴿Or a painful punishment﴾, which is beating with whips. She did not explicitly name Yusuf or say that he had intended evil toward her, because she intended a general statement, that is: whoever intends evil toward your wife deserves to be imprisoned or punished. This is more effective for her purpose of frightening Yusuf. Since she exposed him to imprisonment and punishment, it became obligatory for him to defend himself.

﴿He said: "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself."﴾ Had it not been so, he would have concealed the matter for her and not exposed her. ﴿And a witness from her own family bore witness.﴾ He was her cousin on her father's side. God only placed the testimony on the tongue of someone from her own family so that it would be more binding as proof against her and more reliable in establishing Yusuf's innocence. It was also said that he was her maternal cousin and that he was a baby in the cradle, and his statement was called a testimony because it performed the function of testimony, in that Yusuf's words were confirmed by it and her words were invalidated. ﴿If his shirt has been torn from the front, then she has told the truth, and he is of the liars.﴾

The commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 27:

﴿And if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful.﴾ The implied sense is: a witness testified and said, "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she is truthful, because he hastens after her to catch her and stumbles over the hem of his shirt and tears it; and because he advances toward her while she pushes him away from herself, so his shirt tears from the front." As for the indefinite form of qubul (front) and dubur (back), its meaning is: from a direction that is called qubul, and from a direction that is called dubur. [The commentator] combined "in" (if), which refers to the future, with kana (was), because the meaning is: "if he (the one who checks) knows that his shirt was torn..."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 28:

﴿When he saw his shirt torn from behind﴾ — Qitfir — ﴿he said: Indeed, it is﴾ — that is, your words ﴿"What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your family, except imprisonment or a painful punishment?"﴾ [Yusuf: 25] — or indeed this matter, namely the scheming to attain men, ﴿of your guile﴾ — the address is to her and to her kind — ﴿indeed, your guile is great﴾, because women are more subtle in guile and greater in stratagem, and by it they overcome men. The "qusriyyat" (the women of the palaces) among them have what other women do not have of calamities. And from some of the scholars: "I fear women more than I fear Satan, because Allah Most High said: ﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak﴾ [an-Nisa: 76], and He said to them: ﴿Indeed, your guile is great.﴾"

Yusuf (﴿يُوسُفُ﴾): the vocative particle has been omitted from it, because he is a nearby addressee who is attentive to the conversation, and this implies closeness to him and gentleness toward his station. ﴿Turn away from this﴾ matter, keep it secret, and do not speak of it. Then he said to Ra'il (Ra'ilah, his wife): ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of the mistaken ones.﴾

From among the people who deliberately commit sin. It is said: "khati'a" when one sins deliberately (khati'a: to err or sin intentionally). He used the masculine form of speech by way of giving precedence to males over females. The Aziz was a forbearing man, little given to jealousy, inasmuch as he limited himself to this statement.

﴿And women said﴾ a group of women, and they were five: the wife of the cupbearer, the wife of the baker, the wife of the keeper of the animals, the wife of the jailer, and the wife of the chamberlain. The word "niswah" (women) is a collective singular for "mar'ah" (woman), and its feminine marking is not real (ghayr haqiqi), which is why it is not said "qalat" (she said). It has two dialectal readings: with the nun vowelled with kasra and with damma. ﴿in the city﴾ in Egypt. ﴿the wife of the Aziz﴾ they meant Qitfir. Al-Aziz means "the king" in the language of the Arabs. ﴿She seeks to seduce her young man﴾ her slave. It is said fata-ya and fata-ti, meaning "my young man" and "my servant-girl." ﴿from himself﴾ so that she might obtain her desire from him. ﴿Truly, love for him has pierced her﴾ tamyiz (accusative of specification) (tamyiz, a grammatical term for the accusative that specifies the sense of a preceding word); that is, his love has pierced her, meaning his love has burned through the shaghaf (the membrane covering) of her heart until it reached the inner heart. The shaghaf is the covering of the heart, or a thin skin that is called "the tongue of the heart." (p-١٠٧) ﴿Indeed, we see her in clear error﴾ in mistake and in distance from the path of what is right.

﴿Fa-lamma sami'at﴾ Ra'il ﴿bi-makrihinna﴾ of their scheming, meaning their backbiting (ightiyab) and their saying: "The wife of the al-Aziz has fallen in love with her Canaanite slave, and she has become disgusted with him." The backbiting was called "scheming" (makr) because it is done secretly and in the absence of the person, just as a schemer conceals his scheme. It was also said that she had asked them to keep her secret, but they divulged it about her.

﴿Arsalat ilayhinna﴾ she sent to them, that is, she invited them. It was said that she invited forty women, among them the five mentioned.

﴿Wa-a'tadat﴾ and she prepared and readied. It is from the form ifta'ala, derived from al-'ataad (readiness).

﴿Lahunna muttaka'an﴾ a place of reclining for them, that is, what they would lean upon, such as cushions (namariq). She intended by that arrangement, which is their sitting reclined, while the knives were in their hands, that they would be astonished upon seeing him and occupied away from themselves, so that their hands would fall upon their own hands and cut them, because the one who reclines, when he is stunned by something, his hand falls upon his other hand.

﴿Wa-atat kulla wahidatin minhunna sikkinan﴾ and she gave each one of them a knife. In that era they did not eat except with knives, as the non-Arabs (a'ajim) do.

﴿Wa-qalati ikhruj 'alayhinna﴾ and she said, "Come out before them." The reading with kasr on the ta' (ikhrij) is by Basri, 'Asim and Hamza, and with damm (ukhruj) by the others.

﴿Fa-lamma ra'aynahu akbarnahu﴾ so when they saw him, they exalted him, that is, they magnified him and were overwhelmed by that dazzling beauty and surpassing loveliness. Yusuf's superiority over people in beauty was like the superiority of the full moon on the night of its fullness over the stars of the sky. When he walked through the alleys of Egypt, the radiance of his face was seen reflected on the walls. He resembled Adam on the day his Lord created him. It was also said that he inherited his beauty from his grandmother Sarah.

It was also said that akbarna means they menstruated (hadanna), and the ha' (in akbarnahu) is for pausal (al-sakt), since it is not said that women "hadanahu" (menstruated him), because the verb does not take a direct object. It is said: "akbarat al-mar'ah" when a woman menstruates. Its real meaning is that she entered into maturity (al-kibar), because by menstruation she leaves the limit of childhood. It seems that Abu al-Tayyib took from this interpretation his saying:

"Fear God, and veil this beauty with a face-cover,
For if you appear, the unmarried girls menstruate behind their curtains."

﴿Wa-qatta'na aydiyahunna﴾ and they cut their hands, and wounded them, as you say: "I was cutting the meat, and my hand was cut," meaning it was wounded. That is, they wanted to cut the food that was in their hands, but they were bewildered at what they saw, so they scratched their hands.

﴿Wa-qulna hasha lillah﴾ and they said, "God forbid!" Hasha is a word that conveys the meaning of exoneration (tanzih) in the context of exception. You say: "The people did wrong, except (hasha) Zayd," and it is a particle of the prepositions. It was placed in the position of exoneration and innocence (bara'a). So the meaning of "hasha Allah" is God's innocence and God's exoneration. The reading of Abu 'Amr, "hasha li-llah," is like your saying "saqyan laka" (watering for you), as if he said "bur'an" (innocence), then said "li-llah" to clarify who is being absolved and exonerated. Others read "hasha lillah" by omitting the final alif, and the meaning is the exoneration of God from attributes of incapacity, and the wonder at His power to create a beauty like him.

﴿Ma hadha basharan in hadha illa malakun karim﴾ "This is not a human; this is none but a noble angel." They denied humanity from him because of the strangeness of his beauty, and attributed angelhood to him, and by that they judged what is set in natures: that there is no one more beautiful than an angel, just as it is set in natures that there is no one uglier than the devil.

She said, "That is the one you blamed me for." I (Zulaykha) mean: that is the Canaanite slave whom you saw in yourselves and then blamed me for, meaning: you did not depict him as he truly is; otherwise you would have excused me for being captivated by him. ﴿And I certainly sought to seduce him, but he refused.﴾ The verb isti'sam (refraining, abstaining) is an intensive form (bina' mubalagha) indicating a strong and emphatic refusal and a severe guarding of oneself, as if he were under protection while striving to be further protected. This is a clear indication that Yusuf, peace be upon him, is innocent of what those groups interpreted as the "desire" (hamm) and the "proof" (burhan). Then they said to him, "Obey your mistress." Then Raa'il said, ﴿And if he does not do what I command him,﴾ the pronoun refers to "ma" (what), which is a relative pronoun, and the meaning is "what I command him to do," with the preposition elided, as in His saying "I commanded you the good" (amartuka al-khayr). Or "ma" is a verbal-source particle (masdariyya), and the pronoun refers back to Yusuf, meaning: if he does not carry out my order to him, that is, the requirement and consequence of my command. ﴿He will surely be imprisoned﴾ means he will certainly be jailed. The alif in ﴿and he will surely be among the humiliated﴾ is a substitute for the light emphatic nun (nun al-ta'kid al-khafifa). ﴿Among the humiliated﴾ means together with thieves, runaways and those who shed blood, just as he has stolen my heart, run away from me, and shed my blood through separation. So Yusuf will find no comfort in food, drink or sleep there, just as he has denied me all of that here; and whoever has not been content to be like me, a ruler on a couch in silk, has ended up exhausted on a mat. When Yusuf heard her threat—

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 33:

﴿He said: "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than that to which they invite me."﴾ He attributed the invitation to them (the women), because they said to him: "What harm is there if you obey your mistress, or you are tempted?" Each one of them secretly invited him to herself, so he sought refuge with his Lord. "He said: 'My Lord, prison is dearer to me'" than committing disobedience. ﴿"And unless You turn away from me their scheming, I might incline toward them."﴾ This is a plea from him to Allah, seeking protection (ʿiṣma). ﴿"I might incline toward them"﴾, i.e., I might lean toward them. Ṣabwa (inclination) is leaning toward desire, and from it comes ṣabā (longing), because souls incline toward them for the pleasantness of their fragrance and their delight. ﴿"And I would be among the ignorant"﴾, i.e., among those who do not act upon what they know, because one whose knowledge is of no benefit is like one who has no knowledge, or among the foolish.

Since his words "And if You do not turn away from me their plot" [Yusuf: 33] carried the sense of asking for diversion and supplication, He said, "So his Lord answered him," meaning: God answered his supplication. "And He turned away from him their plot. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing" of the supplications of those who take refuge in Him, "the All-Knowing" of his condition and theirs.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 35:

﴿Then it occurred to them﴾: its subject (fa'il) is implied, due to the indication of what follows and explains it, namely ﴿they would surely imprison him﴾. The meaning is: there arose for them a notion (bada'), i.e., an opinion appeared to them. The pronoun in ﴿to them﴾ refers to the Aziz and his household. ﴿After they had seen the signs﴾, which are the evidences of his innocence, such as the tearing of the shirt, the cutting of the hands, the testimony of the infant, and other things. ﴿They would surely imprison him﴾, in order to display the excuse of the situation and to draw a veil over gossip and talk. But that was only by the urging of the woman upon her husband, and he had been compliant to her and a docile, tractable camel, its halter in her hand. She had hoped that prison would tame him and make him subservient to her, or she feared for him the eyes and suspected the suspicions about him, so shame before the people and fear of the calamity compelled her to accept seclusion in place of the fear of his departure, so that she might be consoled by news of him when she was denied the sight of him. ﴿For a time﴾: until a period, as if she had proposed that he be imprisoned for a while until she could see what would become of him.

﴿وَدَخَلَ مَعَهُ السِجْنَ فَتَيانِ﴾ [And there entered the prison with him two young men.] They were two slaves of the king: his baker (*khabbaz*) and his cupbearer (*sharabiyy*), who had been imprisoned on the charge of poisoning. They were brought into the prison at the same hour that Yusuf was brought in, because the word *ma'a* (مَعَ, "with") indicates companionship (*suhba*). You say, "I went out with the amir," meaning you accompanied him, so their entering the prison must have been as companions of his.

﴿قالَ أحَدُهُما﴾ [One of them said], that is, his cupbearer, ﴿إنِّي أرانِي﴾ [Indeed I see myself], that is, in a dream (p-١١٠). This is a narration of a past state of affairs: ﴿أعْصِرُ خَمْرًا﴾ [pressing wine]. That is, grapes, the word being used for grapes by what they eventually become. Alternatively, *khamr* in the dialect of Oman is a name for grapes.

﴿وَقالَ الآخَرُ﴾ [And the other said], that is, his baker: ﴿إنِّي أرانِي أحْمِلُ فَوْقَ رَأْسِي خُبْزًا تَأْكُلُ الطَيْرُ مِنهُ﴾ [Indeed I see myself carrying bread upon my head, of which the birds eat], ﴿نَبِّئْنا بِتَأْوِيلِهِ﴾ [inform us of its interpretation], that is, the interpretation of what we have seen. ﴿إنّا نَراكَ مِنَ المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ [Indeed we see you to be among the good-doers], meaning among those who excel in interpreting dreams; or among those who do good to the people of the prison, for you cure the sick, console the grieved, and provide generously for the poor. So do good to us by interpreting what we have seen.

It was also said that the two of them had dreamed these dreams to test him. The cupbearer said: "I saw myself in a garden, and behold, there was a vine stem bearing three clusters of grapes. I plucked them and pressed them into the king's cup and gave him to drink." And the baker said: "I saw that upon my head were three baskets containing various kinds of food, and behold, birds of prey were pecking at them."

﴿He said: "No food will come to you as provision that you are given except that I will inform you of its interpretation"﴾, i.e., of the explanation of its reality (māhiyya) and its manner (kayfiyya), because that resembles the explanation of the obscure (tafsīr al-mushkil) ﴿before it comes to you﴾. When they asked him to interpret (their dream) and described him as one of the good-doers, he took the opportunity to describe himself with something that is beyond the knowledge of the scholars, namely informing about the unseen: that he would tell them about the food that would be brought to them in the prison before it reached them, and describe it to them, saying: "Today there will come to you food of such and such a description," and it would be so. He made this a means of transition (takhallus) to mentioning to them the affirmation of God's oneness (tawḥīd), presenting faith to them, making it attractive to them, and making association of partners with God (shirk) repugnant to them. In this there is the point that if a scholar's rank in knowledge is unknown, and he describes himself with what he is qualified for, with the aim that others may benefit from him, this does not fall under self-commendation (tazkiya). ﴿That﴾ is a reference for them to the interpretation, i.e., that interpretation and the informing about hidden matters ﴿is from what my Lord has taught me﴾, and what was revealed to me, and I did not say it from soothsaying or astrology. ﴿Indeed, I have abandoned the creed of a people who do not believe in God, and they are disbelievers in the Hereafter﴾. It is permissible that this be a new independent statement, and that it be a causal explanation of what precedes it, i.e., "He taught me that and revealed it to me because I rejected the creed of those people, who are the people of Egypt and whoever the two youths were upon their religion." (p-111)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 38:

﴿And I follow the religion of my fathers: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.﴾ This is the ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic religion). Their repetition is for emphasis. He mentioned the fathers so that he might show them that he comes from the house of prophethood, after having made known to them that he is a prophet to whom revelation is sent, as shown by what he mentioned of his informing them of the unseen, so as to strengthen their desire to follow his speech. What is meant by it is the abandoning of beginning [shirk], not that he had once engaged in it and then abandoned it.

﴿It is not for us﴾ it is not right for us, we the company of prophets, ﴿to associate anything with Allah﴾ of any kind whatsoever, whether an idol or otherwise. Then he said, ﴿That﴾ tawḥīd ﴿is of the bounty of Allah upon us and upon mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ for the bounty of Allah, so they associate partners with Him and do not desist.

O companions of the prison! (Yā ṣāḥibayi l-sijn)
That is, O you who dwell in the prison, like His saying: ﴿The companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise﴾ [al-Hashr: 20]. ﴿Are many lords divided among themselves better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ He means division in number and multiplicity, i.e.: Is it better for you to have many diverse lords, one of whom enslaves you this way and another enslaves you that way, or for you to have one Lord, the Subduer, who cannot be overcome and has no partner in lordship? This is an example He set forth for the worship of Allah alone and the worship of idols.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 40:

﴿What you worship﴾ is addressed to the two of them and to those among the people of Egypt who follow their religion. ﴿Besides Him﴾ means besides Allah. ﴿Only names that you have named, you and your fathers﴾: that is, you named as gods what does not deserve divinity, then you set about worshipping them; so it is as though you worship only names that have no named realities behind them. The meaning of "sammaytumuhā" (you named them) is "sammaytum bihā" (you named with them), as one says "sammaytuhu Zaydan" (I named him Zayd) and "sammaytuhu bi-Zayd" (I named him with Zayd). ﴿Allah has sent down no authority for them﴾, meaning no proof for their naming. ﴿Judgment belongs only to Allah﴾ in the matter of worship and religion. ﴿Then He explained what He has decreed, saying: "He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion"﴾, the established one to which the proofs point. ﴿But most people do not know﴾. This indicates that punishment applies to the servant even if he is ignorant, when it was possible for him to know the path to knowledge of it.

Then he interpreted the dream, saying: ﴿O two companions of the prison, as for one of you, he will give his lord (i.e., his master) to drink wine﴾. He means the cupbearer. ﴿As for the other, he will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head﴾. It is narrated that he said to the first: "As for what you saw of the vine and its goodliness, it is the king, and the goodness of your situation with him. As for the three branches, they are three days that pass in the prison, after which you will come out and return to what you were upon." And he said to the second: "As for what you saw of the baskets, it is three days, after which you will come out and be killed." When the baker heard of his crucifixion, he said, "I saw nothing." Then Yusuf said: ﴿The matter about which you both inquire has been decided﴾, meaning: it has been cut off and completed, the matter of your inquiry concerning your affair and your state, i.e., the outcome it leads to, which is the destruction of one of them and the deliverance of the other.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 42:

﴿And he said to the one of the two whom he thought would be saved: "Mention me before your lord."﴾ The one who thought (al-zann) is Yusuf, peace be upon him, if his interpretation was by way of ijtihad (independent reasoning). If it was by way of revelation, then the one who thought is the cupbearer (al-shar wabi). Or zann may here carry the meaning of certainty (yaqin).

﴿Mention me before your lord⦆ — describe me to the king by my description and relate my story to him, perhaps he will have mercy on me and deliver me from this predicament.

﴿But Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord﴾ — he made the cupbearer forget. ﴿The mention of his lord﴾ may mean: that he mention him to his lord, or "before his lord," or: Yusuf forgot the remembrance of God when he entrusted his affair to someone other than Him. In a hadith: "May God have mercy on my brother Yusuf. Had he not said, 'Mention me before your lord,' he would not have remained in prison seven years."

﴿So he remained in prison for several years﴾ — that is, seven according to the majority. The word bid' (بِضْع, "several") denotes the range from three to nine.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 12, verse 43:

﴿And the king said, "Indeed I see seven fat cows being devoured by seven lean ones, and seven green ears [of grain] and others withered."﴾ When the relief of Yusuf drew near, the king of Egypt, al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, saw a strange dream that alarmed him. He saw seven fat cows coming out of a dry river, and seven lean cows, and the lean ones swallowed the fat ones. He saw seven green ears whose grain had formed, and seven other withered ones that had been harvested and had ripened. The withered ones twisted around the green ones until they overcame them. So he was troubled by it (*fa-istaʿbarahā*), but he found no one among his people who could interpret it well. It was said: the beginning of Yusuf's trial was in a dream, and then the cause of his deliverance was also a dream.

"*Simān*" is the plural of *samīn* and *samīnah* (fat). *Al-ʿijāf* are the emaciated ones. *Al-ʿajaf* is the emaciation after which there is no plumpness. The reason *ʿijāf* is used as the plural of *ʿajfāʾ*, even though *afʿal* and *faʿlāʾ* are not pluralized on the pattern *fiʿāl*, is that it was treated as the opposite of *simān*. Their practice is to treat a counterpart as analogous to its counterpart, and an opposite as analogous to its opposite. The verse also indicates that the withered ears were seven, like the green ones, because the speech is built on restricting the number to seven in the fat and lean cows and the green ears. Therefore *ukhar* must carry the meaning of seven, and his words ﴿and others withered﴾ mean ﴿and seven others﴾.

﴿O assembly﴾: as if he meant the notables among the scholars and wise men. ﴿Give me your opinion on my dream, if you are able to interpret dreams﴾. The *lām* in *lil-ruʾyā* (for the dream) is the explanatory *lām* (*lil-bayān*), as in His words ﴿and they were of those who were indifferent to it﴾. Or, because the object preceded the verb, it lacks the same strength to govern it as it would if it came after the verb, so it was reinforced with the *lām*. You say *ʿabartu al-ruʾyā* and *lil-ruʾyā ʿabartu*. Or *lil-ruʾyā* could be the predicate (*khabar*) of *kāna* (was), as when you say *kāna fulān li-hādhā al-amr* when he is independent in it and capable of it. *Taʿburūn* is another predicate, or a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause).

The real meaning of *ʿabbartu al-ruʾyā* is that I mentioned its outcome and its final end, just as one says *ʿabartu al-nahr* when one crosses the river until one reaches its far side, which is *ʿabruhu*. Similarly, *awwaltu al-ruʾyā* means that one mentions its *maʾāl*, which is its return. *ʿAbarat al-ruʾyā* with the light form (*takhfīf*) is what the authorities (*al-ithbāt*) have relied upon, and I see them rejecting *ʿabbarta* with the doubled letter (*tashdīd*), as well as *al-taʿbīr* and *al-muʿabbir*.

"They said, 'They are confused dream-visions (adghath ahlam)', meaning: they are jumbled and false things, and what arises from them of the speech of the self (hadith nafs) or the whispering of Satan. The root meaning of adghath is what is gathered of mixed plants and bundles of various kinds of grass; its singular is dighth. It is used figuratively for this, and the construction (idafah) is in the sense of 'min' (of), i.e., 'confused things from dreams'. It is plural though the dream is one, in intensifying the description of the dream as false. It is also possible that they had recounted to him, along with this vision, other visions.' ﴿And we are not versed in the interpretation of dreams﴾. By 'dreams' they meant the false dream-visions, so they said there is no interpretation for them with us; interpretation belongs only to true dreams. Or they acknowledged the shortcoming of their knowledge, and that they were not well-informed in the interpretation of dreams."

"And the one who was saved" from the killing, "of the two" [Yusuf 12:42], from the two companions of the prison, "remembered" — with the dal, which is the eloquent reading — and its origin is idhtakara, so the dhal was replaced by a dal and the ta' by a dal, and the first was assimilated into the second because of the closeness of the two letters. And it is related from al-Hasan: "wa-adhdhakkara," and it was explained that he changed the ta' into a dhal and assimilated it, meaning: he remembered Yusuf and what he had witnessed from him. "After a period" — after a long interval of time. That is because when the king sought interpretation of his dream and its interpretation became difficult for the king, the one who was saved remembered Yusuf and his interpretation of his own dream and that of his companion, and he asked them to let him mention it before the king. "I will inform you of its interpretation" — I will tell you of it, from the one who has its knowledge. "So send me" — and with the ya', Ya'qub reads it: that is, send me forth to him to ask him. So they sent him to Yusuf, and he came to him and said.

﷿ Yusuf, O truthful one (al-Siddiq), O you who are most eloquent in truthfulness. He said this to him because he had tasted and come to know his truthfulness in the interpretation of his dream and the dream of his companion, when he interpreted it as it came to pass: ﴿Yusuf, O truthful one, give us your interpretation concerning seven fat cows which seven lean ones devour, and seven green ears of grain and others dry, that I may return to the people﴾, to the king and his retinue, ﴿that they may know﴾ your merit and your standing in knowledge, so that they will seek you out and free you from your ordeal.
