Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 47:

﴿He said: "You will sow for seven years, consecutively."﴾ This is a statement in the sense of a command, like His saying, ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the cause of Allah﴾. Its evidence is His saying, ﴿leave it in its ear﴾. A command comes in the form of a statement only for emphasis on the existence of what is commanded, so that it is treated as though it already exists, and thus it is reported about. ﴿Da'aban﴾ (consecutively) is read with the hamzah sukun, while Hafs reads it with a vowel. Both are verbal nouns of "da'aba fi al-'amal" (to persist in work), and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to those addressed by the command, meaning: persevering. ﴿So what you reap, leave it in its ear﴾, so that the weevil does not eat it, ﴿except a little of what you eat﴾ during those years.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 48:

﴿Then after that there will come seven hard years, which will consume what you have stored up for them, except for a little that you have set aside.﴾ This is an instance of attribution by metaphor (al-majaz al-isnad, "attribution by metaphor"): the eating of its people has been attributed to the years themselves. ﴿What you have stored up for them﴾ means: in the years of abundance. ﴿Except for a little that you preserve﴾ means: that you keep safe and store away.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 49:

﴿Then after that there will come a year in which the people will be given abundant rain﴾ — that is, after fourteen years, a year. ﴿In it the people will be granted relief (yughath)﴾ — from al-ghawth (relief), meaning their one who calls for help will be answered; or from al-ghayth (rain), meaning they will be rained upon. It is said: "ghithat al-bilad" when the lands were rained upon. ﴿And in it they will press (ya'sirun)﴾ — grapes, olives and sesame, so that they make drinks and oils. "Ta'simun" (you press) is read by Hamzah. He interpreted the fat cows and the green ears of grain as years of fertility, and the lean cows and the dry ears as years of drought. Then, after finishing the interpretation of the dream, he gave them good news that the eighth year would come blessed, abounding in goodness and плентиful in blessings, and that this was by way of revelation.

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me." But when the messenger came to him﴾ to take him out of the prison, ﴿he said, "Return to your lord"﴾, meaning the king, ﴿and ask him what was the matter with the women who cut their hands﴾, meaning, what was the state of the women who cut their hands? Joseph was deliberate and patient in responding to the king, and he put first the question about the women in order to make clear his innocence of what he had been accused of and imprisoned for. This was so that the envious would not use it to disparage his affair before the king, and make it a ladder to lower his standing with him, and so that they would not say that he had remained in prison for seven years only because of a grave matter and a great crime. In this there is evidence that striving (ijtihad, exertion in legal reasoning) to remove accusations is obligatory, as obligatory as avoiding standing in places of suspicion. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We have indeed been amazed at Joseph, at his generosity, his patience, and that God forgives him when he was asked about the lean cows and the fat ones. Had I been in his place, I would not have informed them until I had stipulated that they bring me out. We have also been amazed at him when the messenger came to him and he said, 'Return to your lord.' Had I been in his place and remained in prison as long as he remained, I would have hastened to answer and rushed to the door, and I would not have sought an excuse, if he was indeed forbearing and of patience." From his generosity and good manners is that he did not mention his mistress, despite what she had done to him and the imprisonment and torment she had caused him, and he limited himself to mentioning the women who cut their hands. ﴿Indeed, my Lord knows their plotting﴾, meaning, their scheming is great, and none knows it but God, and He will requite them for it. So the messenger returned to the king from Joseph with his message. Then the king summoned the women who had cut their hands, and summoned the wife of the Aziz, then.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 51:

﴿He said﴾ to them, ﴿"What was your affair when you sought to seduce Yusuf from himself?"﴾ That is, what was your matter, ﴿"Did you find in him any inclination toward you?"﴾

﴿They said﴾ (p-117) ﴿"حاشَ لِلَّهِ"﴾ (Ḥāsha lillāh, "Far be it from Allah") as an expression of amazement at His power to create a chaste character like his, ﴿"We know of him no evil."﴾ That is, no sin. ﴿The wife of the Ruler said, "Now the truth has become manifest"﴾ that is, it appeared and became settled. ﴿"It was I who sought to seduce him from himself, and indeed he is among the truthful."﴾ That is, in his saying, "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself." There is no addition to the two testimonies to his innocence and purity, and to their own admission against themselves that he had not been involved in anything of what he had been accused of.

Then the messenger returned to Yusuf and informed him of the words of the women, and of the acknowledgment of the wife of the Ruler and her testimony against herself.

Then Yusuf said: "That [was so] that he (al-Aziz) may know that I did not betray him in his absence" — that is, my refusal to go out and my insistence on the clearing of my innocence [were so that] he may know. "In his absence" refers to the manifestation of the unseen in respect of his sanctity. The phrase "bil-ghayb" (in the unseen, in absence) is a circumstantial clause (hal) either of the subject (the doer) or of the object, in the sense of "while I was absent from him," or "while he was absent from me." Or [the meaning is]: "that the king may know that I did not betray al-Aziz." "And that Allah" — i.e., and so that he may know that Allah "does not guide the scheme of the treacherous" — does not set it right. This is almost an indirect allusion to his wife and her betrayal of her husband's trust.

Then he wanted to be humble before God and to diminish himself, so that he would not regard himself as pure. He also wanted to make clear that what he had of trustworthiness came through God's guidance (tawfiq) and protection (ʿismah). So he said, ﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾ of slipping (zalal), and I do not testify to his complete innocence, nor do I declare him pure in general circumstances or in this particular incident, because of the concern (hamm) I mentioned, which is the human inclination (khatra bashariyya) and not something arising from deliberate intention and resolve. ﴿Indeed, the self commands to evil﴾. He meant the category: this category commands evil and drives toward it, because of the appetites it contains. ﴿Except what my Lord has shown mercy to﴾: except the part to which my Lord has shown mercy by protection. It is also possible that "mā raḥima" (what) carries the sense of time, meaning: except the time of my Lord's mercy, that is, the self commands evil at all times except the time of protection. Or it is a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), meaning: but my Lord's mercy is what turns away the evil. It has also been said that this is from the speech of the wife of the ʿAzīz, meaning: that which I said was so that Joseph would know that I did not betray him or lie about him in his absence, and that I told the truth about what I was asked. "And I do not absolve myself" (p-118) of betrayal even so, for I did betray him when I accused him and said, ﴿What is the penalty for one who intends evil against your wife except that he be imprisoned?﴾ [Yusuf: 25], and I put him in prison. She intends by this an apology for what she had done. "Indeed every self" ﴿is certainly commanding to evil, except what my Lord has shown mercy to﴾, except a self that God has protected, like the self of Joseph. ﴿Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: she asked her Lord for forgiveness and mercy for what she had committed. This was attributed to the speech of Joseph, though there is no clear evidence for it, because the meaning leads to it. It has also been said that this is an instance of reordering in the Qur'an (taqdim al-Qurʾan wa taʾkhirih), meaning: his saying ﴿That is so that he may know﴾ [Yusuf: 52] is connected to his saying ﴿Ask him what is the matter with the women who cut their hands﴾ [Yusuf: 50].

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 54:**

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself."﴾ I will make him exclusively for myself. ﴿So when he spoke to him﴾ and he witnessed from him what he had not expected, ﴿the king said﴾ to Yusuf, ﴿"Indeed, today you are with us established and trusted."﴾ Of high standing and rank, trusted, entrusted with everything. It is related that the messenger came to him with seventy chamberlains and seventy mounts, and sent to him the garments of kings, and said, "Answer the king." So he came out of the prison and prayed for his family, "O Allah, incline toward them the hearts of the righteous, and do not conceal from them the news, for they are the people most knowledgeable of news about events." He wrote on the gate of the prison, "These are the dwellings of affliction, the graves of the living, the gloating of enemies, and the test of friends." Then he bathed, cleansed himself of the grime of the prison, and put on new clothes. When he entered upon the king, he said, "O Allah, I ask You for Your good through His good, and I seek refuge in Your might and power from His evil." Then he greeted him and supplicated for him in Hebrew (al-'Ibraniyyah). The king said, "What is this language?" He said, "The language of my forefathers." The king spoke in seventy languages, so he addressed him in them, and he answered him in all of them. The king marvelled at him and said, "O truthful one (al-Siddiq), I wish to hear my dream from you." He said, "You saw cows..." and he described their color, their states, and the place from which they emerged, and he described the ears of grain and what was among them in the form that the king had seen. He said to him, "It is your right to gather the food into storehouses (al-Ahra'), so that people will come to you from all directions and seek grain from you, and wealth will be gathered for you that was not gathered for anyone before you." (p-119) The king said, "Who will take charge of this for me, and who will gather it?"

ال­55 – "﴿قالَ﴾" said Yusuf: ﴿اجْعَلْنِي عَلى خَزائِنِ الأرْضِ﴾ "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land," meaning: give me authority over the treasuries of your land, i.e., Egypt. ﴿إنِّي حَفِيظٌ﴾ "Indeed I am trustworthy (amin), I will guard what you entrust to me," ﴿عَلِيمٌ﴾ "knowledgeable" (ʿalim), knowing the ways of managing (al-tasarruf). He described himself with trustworthiness and capability, and these are what kings seek in those they appoint. He said this so that he could attain the enforcement of God's rulings, the establishment of truth, the spreading of justice, and the authority by which the prophets were sent to the servants. And because he knew that no one other than him could take his place in this, he sought it seeking the face of God, not out of love for kingship and worldly life.

In a hadith: "May God have mercy on my brother Yusuf. Had he not said, 'Appoint me over the treasuries of the land,' he would have employed him immediately, but he delayed that for a year." 

They said: this indicates that it is permissible for a person to take up an office (ʿimala) from the hand of an unjust ruler (sultan jaʾir). The predecessors (al-salaf) used to assume the judgeship from the side of oppressors. If a prophet or a scholar knows that there is no way to rule by God's command and to repel injustice except through empowering a disbelieving or wicked king, then he may seek support through him. It was also said that the king used to act upon his opinion and would not object to him in whatever he saw, and he was in the position of a subordinate to him.

﴿And thus﴾, in the same manner of manifest establishment, ﴿We established Joseph in the land﴾, the land of Egypt, which was forty farsakhs (a unit of distance) by forty. Tamkin (establishment) means empowerment and giving capacity. ﴿He settles therein wherever he wills﴾, meaning that every place he wished to make his dwelling was not denied him, because he had gained mastery over all of it and it had come under his authority. "Nashaʾu" (We will): Makki. ﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾, with Our bounty in this world, of kingship, wealth and other blessings. ﴿Whom We will﴾, those for whom wisdom required that We will this. ﴿And We do not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾ in this world. (p-120)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 57:

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe﴾ — meaning Yusuf and others among the believers until the Day of Resurrection — ﴿and they used to be mindful of God﴾, avoiding polytheism (shirk) and grave sins (fawahish). Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: The believer is rewarded for his good deeds in this world and the Hereafter, whereas the wicked person is hastened to receive good in this world, and he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter. Then he recited the verse.

It is narrated that the king crowned Yusuf, sealed him with his ring, girded him with his sword, and placed for him a throne of gold adorned with pearls and rubies. [Yusuf] said: As for the throne, I will strengthen your kingship by it; as for the ring, I will manage your affairs by it; as for the crown, it is not part of my garments nor the garments of my forefathers. So he sat upon the throne, and the kings submitted to him, and the king delegated his affairs to him and dismissed Qitfir. Then [the king] died after that, and [Yusuf] married the king's wife. When he entered upon her, he said: Is this not better than what you sought? He found her a virgin, and she bore him two sons, Afraythim and Misha. He established justice in Egypt, and men and women loved him. The king and many people accepted Islam at his hands. During the years of drought he sold food to the people of Egypt for dirhams and dinars in the first year, until none of them had any left; then for jewelry and gems in the second year; then for livestock in the third year; then for male and female slaves in the fourth year; then for houses and property in the fifth year; then for their children in the sixth year; then for their persons in the seventh year, until he had enslaved them all. Then he freed all the people of Egypt without exception and returned their properties to them. He would not sell to any of the buyers more than a camel's load. The land of Canaan was afflicted with something similar to what Egypt suffered, so Jacob sent his sons to buy grain, and that is His saying.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 58:

﴿And the brothers of Joseph came, and they entered upon him, and he recognized them﴾ without their making themselves known, ﴿but they did not recognize him﴾ because of the change in their appearance, and because he was behind a screen, and because of the long period of time, for he had been forty years away. It is related that when he saw them and they spoke to him in Hebrew (al-ʿIbrāniyyah), he said to them: "Tell me who you are and what your business is." They said: "We are a people from the land of Syria (al-Shām), herdsmen whom hardship has afflicted, so we have come seeking provisions (namtār)." He said: "Perhaps you have come as spies, to look at the weak points of my lands." They said: "God forbid! We are the sons of a prophet, a man grieved over the loss of a son who was dearer to him than us, and he has kept back a brother of his from the same mother, to be company for him." He said: "Bring him to me, if you are truthful."

When he had equipped them with their provisions, he gave each of them a camel-load. It is also read (shādhdh, i.e. an irregular reading) with a kasra on the jīm, as jihāzihim. "He said: Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure, and I am the best of hosts?" [Qur'an 12:59] — "I give full measure" means: I complete it. "And I am the best of hosts": he had treated them generously in lodging and hospitality, and with these words he encouraged them to return to him.

Qur'anic quotations are rendered in ﴿ ﴾ markers as instructed.

﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure (of grain) for you from me﴾, so I will not sell you any food, ﴿and do not come near me﴾. That is: if you do not bring him to me, you will be deprived, and you should not come near me. It is included in the sense of the conditional clause (al-jaza', the apodosis), and is in the jussive mood (majzum), conjoined (ma'tuf) to the grammatical position (mahall) of his words ﴿there will be no measure for you﴾. Or it carries the meaning of a prohibition (al-nahy).

﴿They said: "We will try to get him from his father; and indeed we will do it."﴾ We will deceive him about him and resort to a stratagem until we pull him from his grasp. ﴿"And indeed we will do it."﴾ That is certain; we will not neglect it or be slack about it. He said: "Then leave one of you with me as a pledge." So they left Shim'un (Simeon) with him, and he was the best of them in opinion concerning Yusuf (Joseph).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 62:

﴿And he said to his servants﴾ — Kufan (reading), other than Abu Bakr: "to his youths" (li-fityatihi), others [read it so]. Both (fityan and fityatihi) are the plural of fata (youth), like ikhwa and ikhwan for akh (brother). Fi'lah is used for paucity and fi'lan for abundance, meaning: to his young men who measure out (grain). ﴿Put their merchandise in their saddlebags﴾ — their wares (awi'yatahum); it was sandals, or leather, or silver, and the last is most suitable for slipping into saddlebags. ﴿So that they may recognize it﴾ — they will recognize the obligation to return it and the obligation of generosity in giving the two replacements. ﴿When they return to their family﴾ — and empty out their containers. ﴿So that they may come back﴾ — perhaps their recognition of this will prompt them to return to us; or perhaps they will not find merchandise with which to return; or the piety within them will bring them back to return the trust; or he did not see it as generous to take a price from his father and brothers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 63:

﴿When they returned to their father﴾ with the provisions and told him what had happened, ﴿they said: "O our father, the measure has been withheld from us"﴾ — they mean Yusuf's statement, ﴿"If you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me"﴾ [Yusuf: 60]. Because they had been warned that the measure would be withheld, it was as though the measure had already been withheld. ﴿So send our brother with us, and we will get measure﴾ — we will remove the obstacle to the measure. "Nakhtal" (we will take measure) refers to the provisions we need. "Yaktal" (he will take measure) is read by Hamzah and ʿAli, meaning: our brother will take measure, so that his measuring is added to our measuring. ﴿And indeed, we will be its guardians﴾ — protecting him from anything harmful befalling him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 64:

﴿He said: "Shall I entrust him to you, except as I entrusted his brother to you before?"﴾ That is, you said about Yusuf: ﴿Send him with us tomorrow, he will enjoy himself and play, and indeed we will be his guardians.﴾ [Yusuf: 12] "As you say of his brother, then you betrayed your pledge. So how can I feel secure about him from the like of that?" Then he said: ﴿But Allah is the best guardian,﴾ (Kufi) except Abu Bakr, so he placed his trust in Allah concerning him and entrusted him to them. The word "khayran" is either a circumstantial accusative (hal) or a specification (tamyiz). As for the one who reads "ḥifẓan," it is a tamyiz and nothing else. ﴿And He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾ So I hope that He will bestow upon me His protection of him and not combine for me two calamities. Ka'b said: When he said ﴿But Allah is the best guardian,﴾ Allah the Exalted said: "By My might and My majesty, I will surely return both of them to you."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 65:

﴿When they opened their belongings, they found their merchandise had been returned to them. They said: "O our father, what more could we want? This is our merchandise, returned to us. We will bring provisions for our family, guard our brother, and gain an extra camel-load. That is an easy measure."﴾

Here "mā" (ما) is negative (lil-nafy), meaning: "we do not desire [anything beyond what we have said], nor do we exceed the truth in our speech," or: "we do not desire anything beyond the kindness he has shown us," or: "we do not want from you any other merchandise." Or it is interrogative (lil-istifham), meaning: "What is it that we seek beyond this?"

﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ is a resumptive clause (jumlah mustaʾnafah, a new sentence) explaining their words "what do we desire," and the sentences after it are coordinated with it. That is: our merchandise has been returned to us, so we will strengthen our position with it.

﴿And we will bring provisions for our family﴾ upon our return to the king, meaning: we will bring them grain, which is food carried from a land other than yours (al-mīrah, provisions).

﴿And we will guard our brother﴾ in our going and coming, so that nothing of what you fear befalls him.

﴿And we will gain an extra camel-load﴾: we will gain an extra load (wasq) of a camel by bringing our brother along.

﴿That is an easy measure﴾: easy for him, readily available, not burdensome to him.

﴿He said: "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge before God"﴾. Makki reads ﴿تُؤْتُونِ﴾ (tu'tūnī) with a ya'. ﴿Mawthiqan﴾ means a covenant (ʿahdan) ﴿from God﴾. The meaning is: until you give me what I can rely on as a pledge from God. That is, he wanted them to swear to him by God. He made swearing by God the pledge because swearing by Him is one of the things by which covenants are affirmed, and God had permitted this, so it is a permission from Him. ﴿You will surely bring him to me﴾ is the answer of the oath (jawab al-yamin), since the meaning is: until you swear that you will surely bring him to me. ﴿Unless you are encompassed﴾ means unless you are overpowered and are unable to bring him. Here it is a maf'ul lahu (object of purpose, expressing the reason). The affirmative statement, which is his saying ﴿you will surely bring him to me﴾, is in the sense of a negation, so it must be interpreted as a negation. That is: do not refrain from bringing him except because you are encompassed, meaning do not refrain from it for any reason except one reason, which is that you are encompassed. This is an istithna' min a'amm al-'amm (exception from the most general category, an exception in which the excluded item is taken from the broadest class) in the object of purpose, and an exception from the most general category occurs only in a negative context, so it must be interpreted as a negation.

﴿So when they gave him their pledge﴾. It is said that they swore by God, the Lord of Muhammad, peace be upon him. ﴿He said﴾: some stop here, because the meaning is: Ya'qub said, ﴿God is Witness over what we say﴾ regarding the request for the pledge and giving it. ﴿Wakil﴾ means a watcher, one who is fully aware. However, a pause would separate the speaker from what is said, and that is not permissible. Therefore it is better to distinguish between them by the voice, so that one emphasizes the name of God with the strength of the tone.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 67:

﴿And he said, "O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates."﴾ The majority (al-Jumhur) hold that he feared for them the evil eye (al-ʿayn) because of their beauty and the greatness of their affair, and he did not command them to disperse in the first instance, because in the first instance they were unknown. The evil eye is true in our view. It was argued that Allah the Exalted may bring about, at the moment of looking at a thing and admiring it, a deficiency and a flaw in it. "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to seek refuge for al-Hasan and al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with them both), saying: I seek refuge for you both in the perfect words of Allah from every devil and every harmful eye," [the hadith]. Al-Jubba'i denied the evil eye, and this is (p-124) refuted by what we have mentioned. It was also said that he loved that their enemies should not notice them, lest they plot to destroy them. ﴿And I cannot avail you anything against Allah. The decision is only for Allah. In Him I have put my trust, and in Him let those who trust put their trust.﴾ That is: if Allah intended evil for you, it would not benefit you, nor would it ward off from you what I have pointed out to you of dispersing, and it will certainly befall you. Tawakkul is entrusting the affair to Allah the Exalted and relying upon Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 12, verse 68:

﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾, i.e., dispersed. ﴿It did not avail them against God in anything﴾ their entering by separate gates, i.e., in any way at all, since what befell them, despite their dispersal, was the attribution of theft to them, their exposure because of it, the seizing of their brother when the cup was found in his baggage, and the doubling of the calamity upon their father. ﴿Except for a need﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*), i.e., but rather a need ﴿that was in the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled﴾, namely his compassion for them. ﴿And indeed he was possessed of knowledge﴾, referring to his saying ﴿And I cannot avail you anything﴾ [Yusuf: 67], and his knowledge that caution does not avail against what has been decreed. ﴿Because of what We had taught him﴾, by Our teaching him. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ this.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 69:

﴿When they entered upon Yusuf, he drew his brother to himself﴾. He took Binyamin to himself. It is narrated that they said to him: "This is our brother; we have brought him to you." He said to them: "You have done well." He lodged them and honoured them, then he entertained them, and he seated every two of them at a table. Binyamin was left alone, so he wept and said: "If my brother Yusuf were alive, he would have seated me with him." Yusuf said: "Your brother has been left alone," so he seated him with himself at his table and began to eat with him. He said to him: "Would you like me to be your brother in place of your brother who perished?" He said: "Who would find a brother like you? But Ya'qub and Rahil did not bear you." Then Yusuf wept and embraced him, then ﴿he said﴾ to him: ﴿"Indeed I am your brother, Yusuf"﴾ (p-125). ﴿"So do not grieve"﴾, meaning, do not be sad, ﴿"at what they used to do"﴾ to us in the past. Indeed Allah has been good to us and has gathered us upon good. Do not inform them of what I have informed you. It is also narrated that he said to him: "I will not leave you." He said: "You know the distress of my father over me; if I detain you, his grief will increase, and there is no way to that except that I attribute to you what is not praiseworthy." He said: "I do not mind; do whatever you wish." He said: "I will put my drinking cup into your baggage, then call out after you that you have stolen it, so that I may have a way to bring you back after I have sent you off with them." He said: "Do it."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 70:

﴿When he had furnished them with their provisions﴾ he prepared their requirements and gave them full measure. ﴿He put the drinking-cup (al-siqaya) into his brother's baggage.﴾ The siqaya is a drinking vessel with which one gives drink. It is al-suwa' (the measuring cup/goblet). It is said that the king used to drink with it, and then it was made a measure (sa') by which grain was measured, because food was scarce. It resembled a drinking bowl (tas) made of silver or gold. ﴿Then a caller called out⦆ then a crier called out to them, "azanahu," meaning he informed him, and "adhdhana" means he informed a great deal; from this comes "al-mu'adhdhin" (the muezzin), because of the frequency of this act from him. It is related that they departed, and Yusuf, peace be upon him, gave them time until they had set off. Then he ordered that they be pursued, and they were overtaken and detained. Then it was said to them, ﴿O caravan! Indeed you are thieves.﴾ "Al-ir" (the caravan) refers to the camels that carry the loads, because they "ya'iru," meaning they go and come back; and what is meant is the people of the caravan. ﴿Indeed you are thieves⦆ is a metonymy (kinaya) for their theft of him from his father.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 71–72:

﴿They said, while turning towards them: "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ ﴿They said: "We are missing the drinking-bowl of the king."﴾ It is the sa' (a measure, a drinking vessel). ﴿"And for whoever brings it, there is a camel's load, and I guarantee it."﴾ This is said by the caller (al-mu'adhdhin), meaning: "And I am a guarantor for the load of a camel, which I will pay to whoever brings it." He intended a camel's load of food as a reward (ju'l) for whoever recovers it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 71–72:

﴿They said, while turning towards them: "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ ﴿They said: "We are missing the drinking-bowl of the king."﴾ It is the sa' (a measure, a drinking vessel). ﴿"And for whoever brings it, there is a camel's load, and I guarantee it."﴾ This is said by the caller (al-mu'adhdhin), meaning: "And I am a guarantor for the load of a camel, which I will pay to whoever brings it." He intended a camel's load of food as a reward (ju'l) for whoever recovers it.

"They said, "By God, you know well that we did not come to cause corruption in the land."" This is an oath with the sense of wonder at what was attributed to them. ﴿You know well that we did not come to cause corruption in the land﴾: they called on their knowledge, because of the proofs of their religion and their trustworthiness that had been established in their eyes, since they entered [Egypt] while the mouths of their riding beasts were tied, so that they would not eat crops or food belonging to anyone of the people of the market; and also because they had returned their merchandise (bidā'ah) which they had found in their saddlebags. ﴿And we were not thieves﴾: we were never described as thieves at all.

"They said: What then is the penalty for it" — the pronoun refers to the drinking-cup (al-suwa'): i.e., what is the penalty for its theft, ﴿if you are lying﴾ in your denial and your claim of innocence concerning it.

"They said, 'The penalty for it is: he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself is the penalty for it.'" That is, the penalty for his theft is the seizing of the one in whose saddlebag it was found, and the ruling concerning the thief in the household of Ya'qub was that he be enslaved for a year. Therefore they were asked about his penalty. Their saying ﴿fa-huwa jaza'uhu﴾ ("then he himself is its penalty") is an affirmation of the ruling: that is, the seizing of the thief himself is his penalty and nothing else. Or, "its penalty" is the subject (mubtada'), and the conditional sentence ("he in whose saddlebag it is found...") is its predicate (khabar).

﴿Thus do We requite the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the thieves, by enslavement.

﴿So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother﴾: he began searching their bags before the bag of Binyamin, to clear away the accusation, until he reached his bag. Then he said, "I do not think this one has taken anything." They said, "By God, we will not let him go until you search his baggage, for that is better for your soul and ours." ﴿Then he brought it out﴾, that is, the *suwa'* (the royal drinking cup), ﴿from his brother's bag﴾. The pronoun referring to *al-suwa'* is masculine several times and then made feminine, because the feminine refers to *al-siqaya* (the drinking vessel), or because *al-suwa'* can be used as both masculine and feminine.

The *kaf* in ﴿like this﴾ is in the place of accusative (*mahall al-nasb*), meaning: like that great scheme. ﴿We devised for Yusuf﴾, meaning, We taught it to him. ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾: this is an explanation and clarification of the scheme, because the ruling under the king's law, that is, in his system concerning the thief, was that he be made to pay back twice what he took, not that he be enslaved. ﴿Except that God wills﴾: that is, he could not have taken him except by the will of God and His decree concerning it. ﴿We raise in degrees﴾, with *tanwin* (nunation), is the reading of the Kufans. ﴿Whom We will﴾, that is, in knowledge, just as We raised Yusuf's degree in it. ﴿And over every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾: above him is one of higher rank than he in his knowledge; or, above all the scholars is One who knows, to whom they are inferior in knowledge, and He is God, Mighty and Majestic. (p-127)

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 12, verse 77:**

﴿They said: "If he steals, a brother of his stole before."﴾ They meant Yusuf. It is said that he entered a church (*kaniseh*) and took a small golden statue that they worshipped, and he buried it. It is also said that there was a hen in the house, and he gave it to the one who asked. And it is said: there was a girdle (*mintaqa*) of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, which the eldest of his descendants inherited from one another. Ishaq inherited it, then it passed to his daughter, who was the eldest of his children. She nursed Yusuf, as she was his paternal aunt, after the death of his mother, and she could not bear to be parted from him. When he grew up, Ya'qub wanted to take him away from her, so she resorted to the girdle and fastened it around Yusuf under his clothes, and she said: "The girdle of Ishaq has been lost, so look for whoever took it." They found it tied around Yusuf, and she said: "He belongs to me as a slave (*salam*); I may do with him as I wish." So Ya'qub left him with her until she died.

It is also narrated that when they took out the measuring cup (*al-sa'*) from the baggage of Binyamin, his brothers lowered their heads in shame and turned to him and said: "You have disgraced us and blackened our faces. O sons of Rachel, there is always some calamity from you upon us. When did you take this cup?" Then the sons of Rachel, who were the ones from whom calamity always came upon them, said: "You went away with our brother and destroyed him, and he (Yusuf) placed the cup in the baggage of my brother, just as he placed the merchandise in your baggage."

﴿So he concealed it﴾, that is, their statement: "He stole," as if he had not heard it, ﴿within himself, and did not reveal it to them. He said: "You are worse in position"﴾. The word "in position" is a *tamyiz* (specification), meaning: you are worse in standing regarding theft, because you stole your brother Yusuf from his father. ﴿And Allah knows best what you describe﴾, that is, what you say or what you lie about.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 78:

﴿They said: "O Chief (al-ʿAzīz), indeed he has an aged father, great in years and in rank, so take one of us in his place. Indeed we see you are among the good-doers."﴾ "Take one of us in his place": substitute him, by way of holding as a pledge (al-istirhan) or enslavement (al-istiʿbad), for his father is consoled by him for his missing brother. "Indeed we see you are among the good-doers" to us: so complete your goodness, or it is your custom to be good, so continue in your custom and do not change it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 79:

﴿He said: "We seek refuge in Allah that we should take anyone but him with whom we found our property."﴾ That is: "We seek refuge in Allah, a seeking refuge (ma'aadan) from taking [anyone else]." The verbal noun (al-masdar) is here construed with its object (idafa to the direct object), and "min" (from) is omitted.

﴿Indeed, then we would be wrongdoers.﴾ "Idhan" (then) is a response and a consequence (jawab and jaza') for them, because the meaning is: if we took someone else in his place, we would be wrongdoers. This is because, according to the ruling of your own legal opinion, it is obligatory to take the one in whose baggage the bowl was found and to enslave him. So if we took someone other than him, that would be an injustice by your own school of thought, so why do you demand what you yourselves recognize as injustice?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 80:

﴿فَلَمّا اسْتَيْأسُوا﴾ "They despaired" (يَئِسُوا). The addition of the sīn and the tā᾽ (in اسْتَيْأسُوا) is for emphasis (al-mubālaghah, intensification), as was discussed under اسْتَعْصَمَ. ﴿مِنهُ﴾ "of him," that is, of Yūsuf, and of his answering them. ﴿خَلَصُوا﴾ "they withdrew," they separated themselves from the people, purely, with no one else mixing with them. ﴿نَجِيًّا﴾ "in private consultation": they became people of secret conference (dhawī najwā), or a group conferring privately (fawjan najiyyan), meaning one conferring (munājiyan) for the private consultation of some of them with others. Or, they became entirely given over to private consultation, because they gathered for it and immersed themselves in it with earnestness and concern, as if they were, in themselves, the very form and reality of private consultation. So najī can mean munājī (one who confides), as samīr means musāmir (one who converses at night), and it can also mean the verbal noun, which is al-tanājī (private consultation). Their consultation was about arranging their affair: in what manner they should go, and what they should say to their father regarding their brother?

﴿قالَ كَبِيرُهُمْ﴾ "Their eldest said," in age, and he is Rūbīn (Reuben); or in intellect and judgment, and he is Yahūdhā (Judah); or their leader, and he is Shamʿūn (Simeon). ﴿ألَمْ تَعْلَمُوا أنَّ أباكم قَدْ أخَذَ عَلَيْكم مَوْثِقًا مِنَ اللهِ ومِن قَبْلُ ما فَرَّطْتُمْ في يُوسُفَ﴾ "Do you not know that your father has taken a solemn covenant from you in the name of God, and before this, you neglected Yūsuf?" Here ما is a ṣilah (an added particle with no independent meaning), meaning: and before this you fell short regarding Yūsuf, and you did not keep your father's covenant. Or ما is a verbal-forming particle (maṣdariyyah), and the position of the verbal phrase is nominative as the subject (mubtada᾽), and its predicate is the adverbial phrase, which is "min qabl" (before this). Its meaning: your neglect regarding Yūsuf had occurred before.

﴿فَلَنْ أبْرَحَ الأرْضَ﴾ "So I will not leave the land," that is, I will not depart from the land of Egypt. ﴿حَتّى يَأْذَنَ لِي أبِي﴾ "until my father gives me leave" to return to him. ﴿أوْ يَحْكُمَ اللهُ لِي﴾ "or God judges for me" to leave it, or by death, or by fighting them. ﴿وَهُوَ خَيْرُ الحاكِمِينَ﴾ "and He is the best of judges," because He never judges except with justice.

Return to your father and say, "O our father, your son has stolen." And it is read "surriqa" (was falsely accused of theft), meaning he was attributed with theft. ﴿And we did not testify﴾ against him regarding theft ﴿except by what we knew﴾ of his theft, and we were certain when the bowl was extracted from his bag. ﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾, and we did not know that he would steal when we gave you the solemn pledge.

"Ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came, and indeed we are truthful."

(Ask the town in which we were) — meaning Egypt. That is: send to its people and ask them about the true nature of the matter. (And the caravan in which we came) — and the people of the caravan, who were a people from Kan'an (Canaan), neighbours of Ya'qub (ʿalayhi al-salam). (And indeed we are truthful) — in what we say. So they returned to their father and told him what their brother had said to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 83:

﴿He said: "Rather, your own souls have adorned for you a matter"﴾ that you wanted to do. Otherwise, how would he (the man) have known that the thief is to be enslaved, were it not for your judgment and your teaching? ﴿So patience is beautiful. Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾ — Yusuf, his brother, and their elder ﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing﴾ of my condition in grief and sorrow, ﴿the All-Wise﴾ who has not tested me with this except for a wisdom.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 84:

﴿And he turned away from them﴾, and he turned away from them out of aversion to what they had brought. ﴿And he said, "Oh, my grief over Joseph!"﴾ He attributed the grief (*asaf*), which is the most intense sorrow and regret, to himself. The alif is a substitute (*badal*) for the ya' of possessive attachment (*ya' al-idafa*, the ya' of the first person possessive suffix). The paronomasia (*tajanus*, the close phonetic resemblance between words) between *al-asaf* and *Yusuf* is not artificial, and similar to it are: ﴿What is the matter with you, that when you are told to go forth in the way of God you cling heavily to the earth? Are you content with this life?﴾ [al-Tawba: 38], ﴿and they forbid others from it and keep away from it themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 26], "and they think they are doing good work" [al-Kahf: 104], and ﴿from Saba' with a certain news﴾ [al-Naml: 22].

He grieved over Joseph alone, and not over his brother or their eldest, because his grief over Joseph persisted while the other two were not (so mourned). In this there is evidence that the calamity concerning him, despite the long time that had passed, remained fresh and recent in his heart. ﴿And his eyes turned white﴾, because he wept excessively, and the tears dissolved the blackness of the eyes and changed it into a dim whiteness. It is said that his sight had gone blind, and it is said that he could perceive only faintly. ﴿From the grief﴾: because grief is the cause of the weeping which produced the whiteness, it is as if the whiteness came from the grief. It is said: the eyes of Ya'qub did not dry from the time of separation from Joseph until the time of reuniting with him, eighty years, and there was nobody on the face of the earth more honoured by God than Ya'qub. It is permissible for the Prophet, peace be upon him, (p-130) that his anxiety reach such a degree, because a person is naturally disposed not to control himself at the time of grief, and for this reason his patience was praised. The Prophet (ﷺ) wept over his son Ibrahim and said: "The heart grieves and the eye weeps, and we do not say what displeases the Lord. Indeed, O Ibrahim, we are saddened by you." What is blameworthy is only shrieking, wailing, striking the chest and face, and tearing the garments. ﴿So he was one who suppressed (his grief)﴾: full of suppressed anger over his sons, and not showing what would distress them. Here *kazim* is of the form *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive), as evidenced by His saying: ﴿when he called out while he was suppressing (his anger)﴾ [al-Qalam: 48], from *kazama al-siqa'* (he tied up the waterskin when it was full).

Qur'anic quotation with ﴿ ﴾ markers kept; translate.

﴿They said: "By God, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become (one) wasting away (ḥaraḍan), or you become of those who perish."﴾

Here the meaning is: "Lā tafta'" (you will not cease), with the negative particle dropped, because there is no ambiguity. Had it been affirmative, it would have required the lām and the nūn (the emphatic particles). The meaning of "lā tafta'" is "lā tazāl" (you will not cease to be).

﴿...remembering Joseph until you become ḥaraḍan (a state of being close to destruction through illness)...﴾ or ﴿...become of those who perish.﴾

﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah."﴾ Al-bath (البَثُّ) is the most severe worry that its bearer cannot endure, so he spreads it out to people, that is, he makes it public. He means: I do not complain to any of you or to anyone else. I only complain to my Lord, calling upon Him and seeking refuge in Him. So leave me and my complaint.

It is narrated that revelation came to Ya'qub: "I have only been displeased with you because you slaughtered a sheep, and a poor man stood at your door and you did not feed him. The most beloved of My creatures to Me are the prophets, then the poor. So prepare food and invite the poor to it." It is also said that he bought a slave girl together with her son, then sold her son, so she wept until she went blind.

﴿and I know from Allah what you do not know.﴾ I know from His mercy that He will bring relief to me from where I do not expect. It is narrated that he saw the Angel of Death in his dream and asked him, "Did you seize the soul of Yusuf?" He said, "No, by Allah, he is alive, so seek him." He taught him this supplication: "O Possessor of enduring kindness, whose kindness never ceases and which no one but You can count, relieve me."

O my sons, go and seek out news of Joseph and his brother, ﴿O my sons, go and seek out news of Joseph and his brother﴾ — that is, find out about them and seek information of them. Tahassasa is a form of tafa''ala from al-ihsas (tahassus, "perceiving, sensing"), which is ma'rifah (knowledge, recognition).

﴿And do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ — that is, do not lose hope in the mercy of Allah and His relief.

﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾ — indeed, the matter and the affair is that none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the people who disbelieve. This is because the one who believes knows that he is constantly enveloped in the mercy and blessing of Allah, whereas the disbeliever does not recognize the mercy of Allah or His constant bestowal of blessings, so he despairs of His mercy.

So they set out from their father's presence, returning to Egypt.

"So when they entered upon him" — upon Yusuf — "they said: O Chief (al-'Aziz), adversity (al-durr) has touched us and our family," al-durr meaning emaciation resulting from hardship and hunger. "And we have come with meagre merchandise" — pushed away, which every merchant pushes aside out of disinterest in it and contempt for it; from azjaytuhu, meaning I pushed him away and drove him off. It is said: it was worthless dirhams, not accepted except at a loss; and it is said it was wool and butter. "So give us full measure" — that which is our due — "and be charitable to us" — and show us favour by overlooking the poor quality of the merchandise; or add to our due; or give us our brother. "Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable" (al-mutasaddiqin). When they said, "Adversity has touched us and our family," and humbled themselves before him and asked him to show them charity, his eyes overflowed with tears and he could not restrain himself from making himself known to them, so he said.

"He said: Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother, when you were ignorant?"

Here "هَلْ عَلِمْتُمْ" means: do you know the ugliness (قُبْحَ) of what you did to Joseph, and to his brother, when you were ignorant, not knowing its ugliness? Or it means: when you were in the state of foolishness (السَفَه) and recklessness (الطَيْش). Their treatment of his brother consisted of exposing him to grief by separating him from his full brother (أخيه لأبيه وأمه), and of harming him in various kinds of harm.

﴿Qalū a-innaka﴾ (with two hamzas) is the reading of the Kufans and the Syrians. ﴿la-anta Yūsuf﴾: the lam is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida', the emphatic lam), "anta" is the subject (mubtada') and "Yūsuf" is its predicate (khabar), and the whole clause is the predicate (khabar) of inna. ﴿Qāla anā Yūsuf wa-hādhā akhī﴾. He mentioned his brother, though they had asked him about himself, because mention of his brother was an explanation of what they had asked him about. ﴿Qad manna Allāh ʿalaynā﴾: by bringing us together after separation. He mentioned God's blessing of safety and honour and did not begin with reproach. ﴿Innahu man yattaqi﴾ the indecency (al-fāḥisha), ﴿wa-yaṣbir﴾ from sins and in obedience to God, ﴿fa-inna Allāh lā yuḍīʿu ajra al-muḥsinīn﴾, that is, their reward. He put "al-muḥsinīn" in the place of the pronoun because it includes the God-fearing (al-muttaqīn) and the patient (al-ṣābirīn). It has also been said that "man yattaqi" means whoever fears his Master, and "wa-yaṣbir" means who is patient under his trials; his reward will not be lost in this world or in the next.

"They said, 'By God, God has certainly preferred you over us'": He chose you and favored you over us with knowledge (ʿilm), forbearance (ḥilm), god-consciousness (taqwa), and fine patience (al-ṣabr al-ḥasan). ﴿And indeed we were sinners﴾: and indeed our state and condition was that we were sinners, deliberately committing sin, we did not guard ourselves (with taqwa) and we did not show patience. Undoubtedly (lā jaram), God has exalted you with kingship and humbled us through our submissive supplication (al-tamaskun) before you.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 92:**

﴿He said, "No reproach shall be upon you this day."﴾ That is, no censure upon you. ﴿This day﴾ is governed (*mutaʿallaq*, the word it grammatically depends on) either by *al-tathrib* (reproach) or by *yaghfiru* (forgives). The meaning is: "I will not reproach you this day," and this is the day that is most likely to bring reproach, so what do you think about other days? Then he began and said, ﴿May God forgive you﴾, so he prayed for them that their past wrongs be forgiven. It is said: *ghafara Allahu laka* and *yughfaru laka*, in the form of the past (*al-madi*) and the present (*al-mudari*). Or [the phrase] "This day God forgives you" is a good tidings of God's swift forgiveness.

It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took hold of the two side-posts of the Ka'bah's door on the day of the Conquest and said to the Quraysh, "What do you think I will do with you?" They said, "We think well: a noble brother and the son of a noble brother, and you have the power." He said, "I will say what my brother Yusuf said: ﴿He said, 'No reproach shall be upon you this day.'﴾"

It is also narrated that when Abu Sufyan came to embrace Islam, al-ʿAbbas said to him, "When you come to the Messenger of God, recite to him: 'He said, "No reproach shall be upon you this day."'" He did so, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, "May God forgive you, and whoever taught you."

It is related (p. 133) that when his brothers recognized him, they sent to him: "You invite us to your food morning and evening, and we are ashamed before you because of what we did to you." Yusuf said: "Even if I rule over the people of Egypt, they will still look at me with the former eye, and they will say, 'Glory be to Him who raised a slave who was sold for twenty dirhams to this rank!' Now I am honored by you, since people know that I am from the descendants (*hafadah*, grandchildren or descendants) of Ibrahim."

﴿And He is the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾, that is: if I show mercy to you, and I am the poor one, the stingy (*al-qatur*, the one who withholds), then what do you think of the Rich, the Forgiving?

Then he asked them about the state of their father, and they said, "He has gone blind from excessive weeping." He said, ﴿Take this shirt of mine and go with it,﴾ It is said that it was the inherited shirt that was in Yusuf's amulet, and it was from Paradise. Jibril commanded him to send it to him, for in it is the scent of Paradise, and it does not fall upon one afflicted or sick without his being healed. ﴿Throw it over the face of my father, and he will come back seeing.﴾ "He will become seeing"; you say, "The structure came firm" (jā'a al-binā' muḥkaman), meaning it became firm; or "he will come to me" while he sees. Yahudha said: "Shall I not carry the shirt of healing, just as I carried the shirt of harshness?" It is also said: he carried it barefoot and bareheaded from Egypt to Kan'an, and the distance between them is eighty farsakh. ﴿And bring me all your family.﴾ So that they may enjoy the remnants of my kingdom, just as they grieved over the news of my ruin.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 94:

﴿When the caravan departed﴾ it went out from the encampment (ʿarish) of Egypt. It is said: "fasala (فَصَلَ) min al-balad fusūlan" when one departs from the city and passes beyond its walls. ﴿Their father said﴾ to the son of his son and to those around him from his people. ﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Joseph﴾ Allah caused him to find the scent of the shirt when it arrived from a distance of eight days' journey. ﴿Were it not that you think me senile﴾ al-tafnīd (التَفْنِيدُ) is attributing to someone the condition of al-fanad (الفَنَدِ), which is senility (al-kharaf) and the loss of mental faculties due to old age. It is said: "shaykhun mufannad" (شَيْخٌ مُفَنَّدٌ), meaning an old man whose mind has failed. The meaning is: "Were it not that you condemn me (tafnīdukum iyyāya) as senile, you would have believed me."

"They said: By God, you are surely in your old error." That is, his sons (asbatuh) said it. "Surely in your old error" means: surely in your going astray from the right course of old, in excessive love for Joseph; or in your old mistake concerning the love of Joseph. And they believed that he had died.

﴿When the bearer of good news came﴾, that is, Yahudha (Judah), ﴿he cast it over his face﴾: either the bearer of good news cast the shirt over Ya'qub's (Jacob's) face, or Ya'qub himself cast it over his face. ﴿And he regained sight﴾, meaning he returned to seeing. It is said "radda-hu" and "irtadda," and "irtadda-hu" when he took it back. ﴿He said: Did I not tell you﴾, meaning his saying ﴿Indi la-ajidu rih Yusuf﴾ [Yusuf: 94], or his saying ﴿And do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 87]. His saying ﴿I know from Allah what you do not know﴾ is a fresh statement not governed by the verb "qala" (he said), or it is governed by it. The intended reference is his saying ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know﴾ [Yusuf: 86].

It is reported that he asked the bearer of news: "How is Yusuf?" He replied: "He is the king of Egypt." He said: "What do I want with kingship? On what religion did you leave him?" He replied: "On the religion of Islam." He said: "Now the blessing is complete."

They said, "O our father, ask forgiveness for our sins, for we have indeed been sinners." Meaning: ask Allah to forgive what we committed against you and against your son. Indeed, we have repented and acknowledged our wrongdoings.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 98:

﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾ He delayed the seeking of forgiveness until the time of the pre-dawn (saḥar), or until the night of Friday, or so that he might ascertain their state in the sincerity of their repentance, or until he should ask Yusuf whether he had pardoned them.

Then Yusuf sent to his father a provision (jihaz) and two hundred riding animals (rahilah), so that he might equip himself to come to him with those who were with him. When he reached near Egypt, Yusuf went out, with the king, in four thousand troops, the nobles, and all the people of Egypt, and they welcomed Ya'qub while he was walking, leaning on Yahudha (Judah).

﴿When they entered upon Joseph, he took his parents to himself﴾: he drew them to himself and embraced them. It was said: his mother was still alive. It was also said: she had died, and his father had married her sister, her maternal aunt. The maternal aunt is called a "mother," just as the paternal uncle is called a "father," as in His words: ﴿the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. The meaning of their entering upon him before they entered Egypt is that when he met them, he settled them in a tent-pitching place, or in a palace that he had there. They entered upon him, and he drew his parents to himself. ﴿And he said﴾ to them after that: ﴿Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security﴾, safe from its kings, for they would not enter it except under protection or because of famine. It is narrated that when he met him, Ya'qub (peace be upon him) said: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows." Joseph said to him: "O father, you wept for me until your sight was lost. Did you not know that the Resurrection would gather us?" He said: "Yes, but I feared that your religion would be stripped from you, and I would be separated from you." It is also said that Ya'qub and his sons entered Egypt, and they were seventy-two persons, men and women, and they left it with Musa, and their fighting men were six hundred thousand, five hundred and some seventy men, apart from the offspring and the aged. The offspring were one million and two hundred thousand.

It was said: when they entered Egypt and he sat in his seat of authority, upright on his throne, and they gathered before him, he honored his two parents and raised them onto the throne. ﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾, meaning the eleven brothers and the two parents, prostrating. Prostration was among them a form of greeting and honor, like standing, shaking hands, and kissing the hand. Al-Zajjaj said: the custom of reverence at that time was to prostrate before the one being honored. It was also said that it was only a bowing, without placing the foreheads on the ground, and the words ﴿they fell down in prostration﴾ reject this. It was also said: ﴿they fell down﴾ out of regard for Yusuf, ﴿in prostration to God﴾ in thanks. In this there is also prophethood, and scholars differed about whether they were prophets.

﴿And he said: "O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before. My Lord has made it﴾, i.e. the dream, ﴿true﴾, i.e. truthful." Between the dream and its interpretation there were forty years, or eighty, or thirty-six, or twenty-two.

﴿And He has been good to me﴾. It is said "he was good to him" (aḥsana ilayhi) and "he was good to him in it" (aḥsana bihi), and likewise "he harmed him" (asā'a ilayhi) and "he harmed him in it" (asā'a bihi). ﴿When He brought me out of the prison﴾, and he did not mention the well, because of his words ﴿There is no reproach upon you today﴾ [Yusuf: 92]. ﴿And brought you from the desert﴾, from the badiya (the desert), because they were owners of livestock who moved between water sources and pastures (manāji', plural of man'ja', places where pasture is sought). ﴿After Satan had incited discord between me and my brothers﴾, i.e. he corrupted relations between us and stirred enmity (p-136). ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle (laṭīf)﴾ in what He wills, i.e. subtle in His arrangement. ﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾, in delaying hopes until their appointed terms, or in judging for agreement after disagreement.

﴿My Lord, You have indeed given me of the kingdom﴾, the kingdom of Egypt, ﴿and taught me of the interpretation of events﴾, the tafsir (exegesis) of the books of God or the ta'bir (interpretation) of dreams. The word "min" in both places is for partitive meaning (tab'id), since he was given only part of the kingdom of this world and only part of the interpretation. ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾: it is in the accusative as a vocative (nida'). ﴿You are my guardian in this world and the Hereafter﴾: You are the One who looks after me with blessing in both abodes, and who joins the transient kingdom to the enduring kingdom. ﴿Take my soul as one submitting﴾: he asked to die in a state of Islam, like the saying of Ya'qub to his sons: ﴿And do not die except as Muslims﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102]. It is related from al-Dahhak: "as one sincere (mukhlisan)", and from al-Tustari: "submitting my affair to You (muslimān ilayka amri)". In "'Ismat al-Anbiya'" (The Infallibility of the Prophets) it says: "He only made this supplication so that his people and those after him, who are not assured of their final outcome, would follow him, because the outward conduct of the prophets is what nations look upon." ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾: from among my forefathers, or in a general sense.

It is related that Yusuf took the hand of Ya'qub and walked him through his treasuries. He brought him into the treasuries of gold and silver, the treasuries of garments, and the treasuries of weapons, until he brought him into the treasury of papers. (Ya'qub) said: "My son, how undutiful you are! You have these papers, and you did not write to me for eight stages (of travel)!" He said: "Jibril commanded me." (Ya'qub) said: "Do you not ask him?" (Yusuf) said: "You are more entitled to ask him than I am; so ask him." Jibril said: "God commanded me to do that because of your saying: ﴿and I fear that a wolf will eat him﴾ [Yusuf: 13]. Why did you not fear Me?"

It is also related that Ya'qub remained with him for twenty-four years, then died, and he had instructed that he be buried in al-Sham beside his father Ishaq. Yusuf himself went and buried him there, then returned to Egypt and lived after his father for twenty-three years. When his affair was complete, his soul desired lasting kingship, so he wished for death. It was said that no prophet before him or after him made such a wish. God then took his soul in a good and pure state. The people of Egypt disputed and quarrelled over his burial, each wanting him to be buried in their own locality, until they were about to fight. They then agreed to make a coffin for him of marble, placed him in it, and buried him in the Nile at a place where the water would flow over him and then reach Egypt, so that all of them would share in his blessing (shar'an). Later, after four hundred years, Musa, upon him be peace, transferred his coffin to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Ephraim (Ifraythim) and Micah (Mishya) were born to him, and Nun was born to Ephraim, and Yusha' (Joshua), the young man of Musa, was born to Nun. The Pharaohs, of the 'Amaliqa (Amalekites), inherited Egypt after him, and the Children of Israel remained under their hands, upholding what was left of the religion of Yusuf and his forefathers.

That is (a reference to) what has preceded of the news of Yusuf, and the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿of the news of the unseen which We reveal to you﴾ are the two predicates (khabarani). ﴿And you were not with them﴾ — with the sons of Ya'qub — ﴿when they resolved upon their plan﴾, that is, they determined upon what they intended of casting Yusuf into the well, ﴿while they were scheming﴾ against Yusuf and seeking to bring about calamities for him. The meaning is that this news is unseen (ghayb) and did not reach you except through revelation (wahy), because you were not present with the sons of Ya'qub when they agreed to cast their brother into the well.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 103:

﴿And most of mankind, even though you should strive for it, are not believers﴾

He (Allah) intended generality, or the people of Makkah; meaning: they are not believers, even if you were to exert every effort (ijtihad) upon their faith.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 104:

﴿And you do not ask them for it﴾ concerning the conveying (of the message), or concerning the Qur'an, ﴿any wage﴾, a reward, ﴿It is not but a reminder﴾, that is, it is nothing but an admonition from Allah ﴿to the worlds﴾, and an exhortation to seek salvation, delivered through one of His messengers.

And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth do they pass by, while they turn away from it! (Surah Yusuf 12:105) — the sign here means a mark and an indication pointing to the Creator, to His attributes and to His oneness. "They pass by it" means they pass by the signs, or by the earth, and see them. "While they turn away from it" means they turn away from the signs and do not take heed from them. The intended meaning is what they see of the traces of the destroyed nations and other lessons.

This is the commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 106:

﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah except that they associate others with Him.﴾ That is: most of them do not believe, in their affirmation of Allah and that He created them and created the heavens and the earth, except that they are associators (mushrik) in worshipping the idol. The majority (al-jumhur) hold that it was revealed concerning the polytheists (al-mushrikun), because they affirm Allah as their Creator and Provider, and when a severe matter afflicts them they call upon Allah, yet along with that they associate others with Him. Among the forms of shirk is what the Qadariyya (al-Qadariyya, the sect that affirmed human power to create) say, namely affirming the power of creation (qudrat al-takhliq) for the servant. And pure monotheism (al-tawhid al-mahd) is what Ahl al-Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the Sunni community) say, which is that there is no creator except Allah.

Are they then secure from an overwhelming punishment from God's chastisement reaching them, or the Hour coming upon them suddenly while they do not perceive its approach? (Commentary of al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil)

Wait, I must translate faithfully rather than paraphrase. Here is the corrected translation:

﴿Are they then secure that there will not come upon them an overwhelming (ghashiyah) — a punishment that envelops them and encompasses them — from the chastisement of God, or that the Hour (al-sa'ah) — the Resurrection — will not come upon them suddenly (baghtatan), while they do not perceive (la yash'urun) its coming?﴾

Note on the grammar: "baghtatan" is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), meaning "suddenly," i.e., "faj'atan." "Wa hum la yash'urun" is the situational clause, meaning "while they are unaware of its coming."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 108:

﴿Say: This is my way.﴾ This is the way, which is the call to faith and to tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), is "my way." The words sabil (way) and tariq (path) may be treated as masculine or feminine. Then he explained "his way" with his words ﴿I call to God with insight.﴾ That is: I call to His religion with clear proof, not blind. ﴿I⦁﴾ is an emphatic restatement of the pronoun hidden in "I call" (adu). ﴿And whoever follows me﴾ is a conjunction with it, meaning: I call to the way of God, I and whoever follows me also calls to it. Or, "I" is the subject (mubtada') and "with insight" is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and "and whoever follows me" is a conjunction with "I," informing at the outset that he and whoever follows him act upon proof and evidence, not upon whim. ﴿And glory be to God﴾: I exalt Him above partners. ﴿And I am not of the polytheists﴾: I do not associate anything else with God.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 109:

﴿We did not send before you except men﴾, not angels, because they used to say, ﴿If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [41:14]. Or [it means]: were there not women among them? ﴿We revealed﴾, with the nun (نُوحِي, nuḥī) read by Ḥafṣ, ﴿to them from the people of the towns﴾, because they were more knowledgeable and more forbearing, whereas the people of the desert had ignorance and coarseness. ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them? And the abode of the Hereafter﴾, that is: "and the abode" of the Hour, "the Hereafter," ﴿is better for those who guard against [shirk]﴾ and believe in it. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ With the ya' (يَعْقِلُونَ, yaʿqilūn, "they reason") read by Makkī, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah and ʿAlī. (p-١٣٩)

﴿Until, when the messengers despaired﴾ of the faith of the people, ﴿and they thought that they had been denied﴾. The messengers were certain that their people had denied them. As for the light reading (al-takhfif, reading the verb without doubling its middle consonant), it is that of the Kufan reader, meaning: the one sent to them thought that the messengers had been denied, i.e., had been broken faith with (أُخْلِفُوا). Or it means: the one sent to them thought that they had been denied on the part of the messengers, i.e., the messengers had lied to them about their being victorious over them, and they had not believed them in this.

﴿Our help came to them﴾ for the prophets and those who believed in them, suddenly and unexpectedly. ﴿So whomever We willed was saved﴾: with a single nūn, a doubled jīm and a fatḥah on the yā' is the reading of the Syrian reader (Ibn 'Amir) and 'Asim, in the form of the past tense built for the passive (mabni lil-maf'ul, the verb form whose subject is not named), and the deputy of the subject (nā'ib al-fā'il) is "man." The rest read "fa-nunjī" with two nūns, the second one silent and concealed before the jīm that follows it, and the yā' with sukūn. ﴿Whom We willed﴾ means the Prophet and whoever believed in him. ﴿And Our punishment is not turned back﴾ (i.e., Our chastisement) ﴿from the guilty people﴾, the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 12, verse 111:

﴿Indeed, there was in their stories﴾ i.e., in the stories of the prophets and their peoples, or in the story of Yusuf and his brothers, ﴿a lesson for people of understanding﴾, in that he was transferred from the height of love to the depths of the well, and from the mat to the couch; so the outcome of patience became safety and honour, and the end of deceit became ruin and remorse. ﴿It was not a narration that could be invented﴾: the Qur'an was not an invented narrative, as the disbelievers claimed. ﴿But it is a confirmation of what came before it﴾: but it is a confirmation of the Books that preceded it, ﴿and a detailed explanation of all things﴾ that are needed in religion, for it is the foundation (qanun) upon which the Sunnah (the prophetic tradition), the consensus (ijma') and analogy (qiyas) rest. ﴿And a guidance﴾ from misguidance, ﴿and a mercy﴾ from punishment, ﴿for a people who believe﴾ in Allah and His prophets. What is put in the accusative after "lakin" (but) is coordinated with the predicate of "kana" (was). (p-140)

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Teach your slaves the Surah of Yusuf, for whichever slave recites it and teaches it to his family and to those whom his right hand possesses, Allah will make the agonies of death easy for him and will grant him the strength not to envy a Muslim."

The Shaykh Abu Mansur, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The mention of the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and his brothers is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning the harm of the Quraysh, as if it is saying: the brothers of Yusuf, despite their agreement with him in religion and despite the kinship, did to Yusuf what they did of plotting and deceit, and he endured that; so you, despite their opposition to you in religion, are more deserving to endure their harm."

Wahb said: Allah, exalted is He, did not send down any Book except that it contained the Surah of Yusuf, peace be upon him, complete as it is in the Mighty Qur'an. And Allah knows best.
